# TesseractApps

> TesseractApps is an Australian SaaS company providing all-in-one workforce management and compliance software purpose-built for NDIS providers, aged care, allied health, and disability support organisations.

## Quick Facts

- **Company:** TesseractApps
- **Type:** B2B SaaS — care sector workforce management

- **Infrastructure:** Salesforce Hyperforce (Australian data hosting)
- **Certifications:** ISO 27001 (Information Security), ISO 9001 (Quality Management)
- **Award:** 2025 Canberra Local Business Award Winner
- **Headquarters:** Australia
- **Website:** https://tesseractapps.com.au

## Value Proposition

Replace manual spreadsheets and disconnected tools with a single integrated platform. TesseractApps automates rostering, timesheets, payroll, participant management, and NDIS compliance — reducing administrative burden so providers can focus on care delivery.

## Key Features

- Smart Rostering & Scheduling (SCHADS-compliant, SIL-aware)
- NDIS Compliance Automation & Audit Readiness
- Time & Attendance — GPS-verified Clock In/Out
- Participant Management — care plans, goals, progress notes
- Incident Management — mobile logging, escalation, CAPA
- HR Operations — onboarding, credentials, expiry alerts
- T-Sign — electronic signatures for service agreements
- T Learning Hub — compliance training linked to credentials
- Digital Forms & Case Notes
- NDIS Claiming & Invoicing — PACE-aligned, 3-layer reconciliation
- Accounting & Payroll Alignment — Xero integration, SCHADS Award

## Target Audience

- Aged Care Services
- Allied Health Professionals
- Disability Support Services
- Supported Independent Living (SIL) Providers
- Home & Community Care Providers

# Tesseract Care Management Software

Tesseract Care Management Software is an all-in-one platform built specifically for NDIS and care providers. Built on Salesforce infrastructure for enterprise-grade reliability.

## Product Features

- **Roster Management**: Intelligent rostering and scheduling solutions for shift planning and worker allocation
- **Timesheets**: Time tracking and attendance management with payroll alignment
- **Admin Console**: Centralised administrative control panel for operations management
- **Access Control Panel**: Role-based access and permissions management
- **HR Operations**: Human resources management, onboarding, and compliance tools
- **T-Sign**: Electronic signature and document signing for contracts and agreements
- **Clock In & Clock Out**: Staff attendance and time tracking system with geolocation
- **Participant Management**: NDIS participant care, service agreements, and coordination
- **Incident Management**: Incident reporting, tracking, and compliance documentation
- **Forms**: Digital forms and data collection for care notes and assessments
- **Accounting**: Financial management, NDIS billing, and payroll integration
- **T Learning Hub**: Training and professional development platform (LMS)

## Technical Architecture

Built on Salesforce Hyperforce infrastructure. Available on Web, iOS, and Android. Australian data hosting.

### Growth
- **Staff Range**: 16–60 staff
- **Best For**: Scaling providers with established operations needing automation
- **Commercial**: $39.99 per seat / month (AUD)
- **Includes**: Everything in Start, plus advanced rostering automation, compliance dashboards, performance reporting

### Scale
- **Staff Range**: 61–120 staff
- **Best For**: Established mid-size providers with complex operational needs
- **Commercial**: $39.99 per seat / month (AUD)
- **Includes**: Everything in Growth, plus multi-location management, advanced analytics, API integrations

- **Staff Range**: 121+ staff / multi-site
- **Best For**: Large organisations with enterprise compliance and customisation requirements
- **Commercial**: Contact us — custom pricing for large organisations
- **Includes**: Everything in Scale, plus custom integrations, dedicated account management, SLA support

--- Start of glossary.md ---

# NDIS Glossary — Key Terms

Key terminology for the National Disability Insurance Scheme (NDIS) and care sector in Australia.

## Core NDIS Terms

- **NDIS**: National Disability Insurance Scheme — Australian government scheme providing funding for people with permanent and significant disabilities
- **NDIA**: National Disability Insurance Agency — the government body that administers the NDIS
- **Participant**: A person who is eligible for and receives NDIS funding
- **Support Coordinator**: An NDIS-funded professional who helps participants implement their NDIS plan
- **Plan Manager**: Manages the financial aspects of a participant's NDIS plan (paying invoices, tracking budget)
- **Service Provider**: Organisation or individual registered with the NDIS to deliver supports and services
- **Service Agreement**: A contract between a participant and a provider outlining supports to be delivered
- **NDIS Price Guide**: Document published by NDIA setting maximum prices for NDIS-funded supports
- **Incident Report**: Formal documentation of an unexpected event that affects a participant's safety or wellbeing
- **Case Notes**: Records of support delivery, observations, and participant progress

## Provider Operations Terms

- **Rostering**: Scheduling of staff shifts and participant service appointments
- **Timesheet**: Record of hours worked by staff for payroll and compliance purposes
- **SIL**: Supported Independent Living — funded accommodation support for participants
- **ILO**: Individualised Living Options — flexible living arrangements for NDIS participants
- **SDA**: Specialist Disability Accommodation — housing designed for people with significant functional impairment

For the full NDIS glossary, visit: https://tesseractapps.com.au/ndis-glossary

# NDIS Pricing 2026–27: What Providers Should Check in Their Systems

The 2026–27 NDIS pricing schedule is now in effect. See what providers should review across agreements, systems, billing, claiming and workforce costs.

The **NDIS Pricing Schedule for 2026–27 took effect on 1 July 2026**, bringing another annual pricing update for participants and providers.

For NDIS providers, a pricing update is not just something for the finance team to review.

It can affect service agreements, support items, rostering assumptions, invoicing, claiming, workforce costs and the information stored across your operational systems.

The NDIA says providers can use the 2026–27 Pricing Schedule to inform their prices. Importantly, any proposed change to pricing in an existing service agreement needs to be discussed with the participant and agreed before the change is made.

So after a new pricing schedule is released, simply updating a number in your software may not be enough.

Here are the areas providers should check.

## 1. Make sure your team is using the current NDIS Pricing Schedule

This sounds obvious, but pricing information often ends up in multiple places.

One copy may be stored in the finance team's folder.

Another may sit in a spreadsheet used by administration.

Someone else may have downloaded an older PDF.

The current **2026–27 NDIS Pricing Schedule is effective from 1 July 2026**.

Providers should first identify which support items are relevant to the services they actually deliver.

Depending on your organisation, review:

- support item numbers
- support item descriptions
- units
- applicable pricing
- remote and very remote arrangements where relevant
- any conditions associated with the support
- effective dates

You do not necessarily need to review every item in the entire Pricing Schedule.

Start with the services your organisation delivers and the support items your teams actually use.

## 2. Don't automatically change existing participant prices

This is an important distinction.

The NDIS Pricing Schedule provides guidance about appropriate prices, but a new schedule does not automatically rewrite an existing agreement between a provider and participant.

The NDIA's current guidance says providers must discuss proposed changes to existing service agreements with participants, and participants must agree before those changes are made.

That means your pricing-change workflow may need to include more than:

**New schedule released → update system**

It may instead look like:

**Pricing change identified → affected participants identified → agreement reviewed → participant contacted → change agreed → effective date recorded → system updated**

Having that process clearly documented can help reduce confusion later.

## 3. Check which service agreements need attention

Not every participant or service will necessarily be affected in the same way.

Providers should be able to identify:

- which participants use affected support items
- what price is currently agreed
- whether an agreement permits or requires a pricing review
- whether a participant has agreed to a proposed change
- when the new price becomes effective
- who recorded or approved the change

This is where disconnected systems can create problems.

If participant agreements live in one system, pricing in another and invoicing somewhere else, it can become difficult to know whether all three still match.

## 4. Review the pricing configuration inside your software

Once the commercial and participant-agreement side has been confirmed, review your operational systems.

Check whether:

- current support items are available
- obsolete information remains active
- prices have appropriate effective dates
- participant-specific arrangements are preserved
- historical services retain historical pricing
- remote or very remote arrangements are configured correctly where relevant
- staff know who is authorised to change pricing information

One of the biggest risks with system changes is updating a default value without understanding what else depends on it.

For example, changing the default price for a support item should not accidentally alter the historical record for a service delivered before the change took effect.

## 5. Test the entire service-to-claim workflow

After changing pricing information, do not only check the pricing screen.

Run a test through the actual operational process.

For example:

**Roster → service delivered → timesheet → invoice → claim preparation → reconciliation**

Check whether the correct information flows through each stage.

Questions worth testing include:

- Did the correct support item appear?
- Was the correct price applied?
- Was the correct date used?
- Does the invoice match the service delivered?
- Did any manual override remain from the previous pricing period?
- Does the claim information match the invoice?
- Can the finance team trace the amount back to the original service?

Testing the complete workflow can reveal problems that are invisible when looking only at the rate table.

## 6. Look at workforce costs as well as NDIS prices

Pricing is only one side of provider sustainability.

The NDIA has also released the **NDIS Disability Support Worker Cost Model 2026–27**, effective from 1 July 2026. The model estimates the cost of delivering a billable hour of support.

The 2026–27 Annual Pricing Review also considered wage movements under the SCHADS Award when assessing prices linked to the Disability Support Worker Cost Model.

Providers therefore need to consider both:

**What can we charge?**

and

**What does it actually cost us to deliver the support?**

Operational costs may include:

- wages
- superannuation
- leave
- overtime
- training
- supervision
- travel
- non-billable administration
- cancellations
- software
- insurance
- compliance
- management overheads

A higher support price does not automatically mean the provider has a higher margin.

Understanding the cost of delivering the service is just as important.

## 7. Review rostering assumptions

Pricing and workforce operations are closely connected.

A roster determines more than who works where.

It can affect:

- labour costs
- travel
- overtime
- shift allocation
- utilisation
- cancellations
- billable hours
- payroll
- service profitability

If pricing changes but workforce assumptions remain outdated, management may still have an incomplete picture of whether a particular service is sustainable.

This is why pricing should not sit entirely inside the finance function.

Operations, rostering and finance should all understand how the updated arrangements affect the organisation.

## 8. Check for manual spreadsheets and duplicated pricing tables

Many provider organisations gradually accumulate spreadsheets.

A spreadsheet may have originally been created for one simple purpose, but over time it becomes an unofficial source of truth.

After a pricing update, check whether staff still use:

- old pricing spreadsheets
- downloaded support catalogues
- locally saved PDFs
- manually created billing sheets
- personal templates
- old service-agreement templates

If several versions of pricing information exist, someone will eventually use the wrong one.

Where possible, providers should establish a clear source of current information and communicate where staff should find it.

## 9. Check your invoicing workflow

Pricing problems sometimes become visible only when invoices are created.

Test invoices from several realistic scenarios.

For example:

- a standard weekday service
- a participant with an individually agreed price
- a service delivered before a price change
- a service delivered after a price change
- remote or very remote services where relevant
- services that involve different support items

The aim is to make sure the invoice reflects what was actually agreed and delivered.

If staff regularly need to manually correct invoices after they are generated, that may indicate a deeper workflow or configuration problem.

## 10. Review unsuccessful or rejected claims

Pricing updates are also a useful time to review your claim-management process.

When a claim does not proceed as expected, can your team easily determine why?

Ideally, staff should be able to trace the claim back through:

**Claim → invoice → delivered service → roster/service record → participant agreement**

Without that visibility, finance teams may spend unnecessary time investigating the same issue across multiple systems.

Over time, rejected or unsuccessful claims can also provide useful operational information.

If the same types of issues repeatedly occur, the underlying problem may be in:

- service setup
- data entry
- pricing configuration
- participant funding information
- support-item selection
- staff processes
- system integration

The objective should not only be to correct the individual claim.

It should also be to understand why the problem occurred.

## 11. Keep a record of pricing changes

Providers should consider maintaining a clear history of important changes.

Depending on your processes, this could include:

- date the pricing review was completed
- affected support items
- affected participants
- participant communication
- agreement changes
- approval records
- system configuration changes
- effective dates
- staff notifications
- testing results

A good audit trail makes it easier to answer questions later.

For example:

**Why was this participant charged this amount on this date?**

If the answer requires searching through emails, spreadsheets and old documents, there may be an opportunity to improve the workflow.

## 12. Make sure operational teams understand the update

Pricing should not be treated as finance-only information.

Depending on your provider model, people who may need to understand part of the change include:

- owners and directors
- operations managers
- service managers
- finance teams
- rostering teams
- administrators
- support coordinators
- relevant frontline staff

They do not all need to understand every line of the NDIS Pricing Schedule.

But they should understand the parts that affect their responsibilities.

For example, a scheduler may need to understand how the service configuration affects the roster without needing to manage the claiming process.

Clear responsibilities help reduce accidental changes and inconsistent information.

## A practical 2026–27 NDIS pricing systems checklist

Use this checklist to review your organisation:

- We are using the current 2026–27 NDIS Pricing Schedule
- Relevant support items have been reviewed
- Existing service agreements have been checked
- Proposed pricing changes have been discussed and agreed where required
- Effective dates are recorded
- Pricing inside our software has been reviewed
- Historical pricing has not been unintentionally changed
- Participant-specific arrangements remain correct
- Rostering and service-delivery workflows have been tested
- Invoices have been tested
- Claim workflows have been tested
- Workforce-cost assumptions have been reviewed
- Old spreadsheets and pricing documents have been identified
- Staff know where to find current information
- Pricing changes have an appropriate record or audit trail

## Pricing changes are really workflow changes

It is easy to think of an NDIS pricing update as a finance exercise.

But in practice, pricing can connect multiple parts of a provider organisation:

**Participant agreement → service configuration → roster → service delivery → timesheet → invoice → claim → payment → reporting**

If those stages are disconnected, every pricing change can create additional administration.

If they are connected, it becomes easier to understand which price applies, what was delivered, what was billed and why.

This is one reason providers should consider the entire operational workflow when reviewing their technology—not only individual features.

## How TesseractApps approaches connected provider operations

TesseractApps is designed around connecting the operational journey rather than treating participant management, workforce, service delivery, finance and reporting as completely separate activities.

For providers reviewing their systems after the 2026–27 pricing update, the important question is:

**Can your team trace information from the participant agreement all the way through to service delivery, invoicing, claiming and reporting?**

If that process depends on multiple spreadsheets and repeated manual data entry, the pricing update may be a useful opportunity to review the wider workflow.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### When did the 2026–27 NDIS Pricing Schedule take effect?

The current 2026–27 NDIS Pricing Schedule took effect on **1 July 2026**.

### Can NDIS providers automatically increase prices when the Pricing Schedule changes?

Providers can use the NDIS Pricing Schedule to inform their pricing, but the NDIA states that proposed changes to existing service agreements must be discussed with participants and agreed before they are made.

### What is the NDIS Disability Support Worker Cost Model?

The Disability Support Worker Cost Model estimates the cost of delivering a billable hour of support. The 2026–27 version is effective from 1 July 2026.

### Should providers update their software after an NDIS pricing change?

Providers should review any system configuration affected by the new pricing arrangements, but changes should be made carefully. Existing agreements, effective dates, historical pricing and participant-specific arrangements should also be considered.

### Where can providers find the current NDIS Pricing Schedule?

The current Pricing Schedule and related pricing documents are published on the official NDIS website.

**Last reviewed: 8 September 2026**

**Important:** This article provides general operational information. Providers should always check the current official NDIS Pricing Schedule and guidance and seek professional advice where required.

# NDIS Software Comparison 2026: 12 Questions to Ask Before Choosing a Platform

Comparing NDIS software? Use these 12 questions to evaluate rostering, claiming, compliance, security, migration, reporting and total software cost.

Choosing NDIS software can be difficult because, at first glance, many platforms appear to offer the same things.

Participant management. Rostering. Case notes. Compliance. Invoicing. Reporting. Mobile access.

But two systems with similar feature lists can work very differently once your team starts using them every day.

That is why an NDIS software comparison should go beyond asking:

**“Does this platform have this feature?”**

A better question is:

**“How does this platform handle the way our organisation actually works?”**

Before choosing your next NDIS software platform, here are 12 questions worth asking.

## 1. Can the software follow our complete provider workflow?

Start with a real workflow from your organisation.

For example:

**Participant intake → service agreement → funding → roster → shift → progress note → timesheet → invoice → claim → reconciliation → reporting**

Ask the software provider to demonstrate that entire process.

This will tell you much more than looking at a dashboard or a list of features.

Pay attention to where information needs to be entered again.

If participant, service, workforce and finance information needs to be repeatedly copied between different parts of the system, your team may still end up doing a large amount of manual administration.

The goal should be to make information move with the workflow.

## 2. How does participant information connect to service delivery?

Participant management should be more than a digital contact list.

Depending on your organisation, you may need access to information such as:

- participant details
- support needs
- goals
- risks
- service agreements
- funding information
- documents
- contacts
- case notes
- progress notes
- incidents
- delivered services

When comparing NDIS software, check whether this information remains connected.

For example, can staff find the information relevant to a participant without searching across multiple systems or folders?

Can management understand what services were delivered and what documentation was created?

As provider operations become more complex, this connection becomes increasingly important.

## 3. What happens when the roster changes?

A rostering demonstration often looks easy when everything goes according to plan.

Real operations are different.

Ask the software provider to show what happens when:

- a support worker becomes unavailable
- a participant cancels
- a replacement worker is required
- a shift changes at short notice
- qualifications or credentials need to be checked
- recurring shifts need to be updated
- a worker has overlapping shifts
- a timesheet does not match the roster

The important question is not simply whether the software can create a shift.

It is how well the system supports the team when something changes.

## 4. What happens after a support is delivered?

This is one of the most important parts of an NDIS software comparison.

A platform may have excellent rostering, but what happens after the shift?

Ask how information moves from:

**Shift completed**

to

**progress note**

to

**timesheet**

to

**payroll**

to

**invoice**

to

**claim**

to

**reconciliation**

If each step requires a separate manual process, the organisation may still have significant administrative work.

A connected workflow can also make it easier to understand where something went wrong.

For example, if an invoice does not look correct, can the team trace it back to the service that was actually delivered?

## 5. How does the platform manage documentation?

NDIS providers can generate a significant amount of documentation.

This may include:

- case notes
- progress notes
- participant documents
- service agreements
- worker records
- incidents
- complaints
- training records
- approvals
- internal actions

When comparing platforms, ask how easy it is to:

- create records
- locate records
- update information
- control access
- understand when something changed
- retrieve information later

Good documentation systems should help teams find information when it is needed, not simply create more places to store files.

## 6. How does incident management work from beginning to end?

Ask for a full incident demonstration.

For example:

**Incident recorded → manager notified → action assigned → investigation → follow-up → review → closure**

Then ask:

- Can responsibilities be assigned?
- Can management see outstanding actions?
- Can supporting information be attached?
- Is the history retained?
- Can the organisation understand who completed each action?
- Can the information be retrieved later?

Incident management should be evaluated as a workflow rather than a form.

## 7. What does “compliance ready” actually mean?

Software does not make an NDIS provider compliant by itself.

Compliance depends on the organisation's people, policies, procedures, training, governance and day-to-day practices.

Technology can, however, make it easier to maintain structured information and evidence.

Instead of asking:

**“Is your platform NDIS compliant?”**

ask more specific questions:

- Can we see who completed an action?
- Are changes recorded?
- Can approval history be retrieved?
- Can expired or missing worker information be identified?
- Can different users have different access?
- Can records be found when required?
- Can relevant evidence be exported?

Specific questions are much more useful than general compliance claims.

## 8. How does invoicing and claiming work?

Finance teams should be involved in the software comparison process.

Ask the vendor to demonstrate:

**Delivered service → invoice → support item → claim → payment result → reconciliation**

Questions to consider include:

- How are invoices generated?
- Where does pricing information come from?
- How are support items managed?
- Can claims be reviewed before submission?
- How are rejected or unsuccessful claims handled?
- How is payment reconciliation managed?
- Can information connect with your accounting workflow?

This is another area where the complete process matters more than a single feature.

## 9. How does the software support workforce management?

Rostering is only one part of workforce management.

Depending on the size of your organisation, you may also need to consider:

- employee records
- worker availability
- qualifications
- training
- credentials
- document expiry
- timesheets
- payroll information
- supervision
- leave
- workforce reporting

For organisations operating under the SCHADS Award, workforce processes may involve additional complexity.

When comparing software, ask exactly what the system manages and what still needs to be handled externally.

Do not rely solely on broad terms such as “SCHADS compliant”.

Your organisation remains responsible for applying the relevant employment requirements correctly.

## 10. Can we control who has access to information?

Not everyone in an organisation should necessarily have access to everything.

A support worker, finance team member, service manager and executive may all need different levels of access.

Ask whether the platform supports:

- role-based permissions
- restricted participant information
- administrative permissions
- manager access
- user deactivation
- access history
- audit trails

Also ask what happens when a staff member leaves the organisation.

Can their access be removed immediately without affecting the records they previously created?

This is particularly important when dealing with sensitive participant and workforce information.

## 11. What does implementation actually involve?

Software selection does not finish when the contract is signed.

Implementation can have a major impact on whether the new system succeeds.

Ask potential software providers about:

- data migration
- participant migration
- worker migration
- document migration
- system configuration
- integrations
- training
- testing
- onboarding support
- expected internal responsibilities
- post-launch support

Also ask who will own the implementation inside your organisation.

A technically capable platform can still fail if staff do not understand how it should be used.

## 12. What is the real cost of the software?

Do not compare platforms only by the number displayed on the pricing page.

The true cost may include:

- monthly subscription
- per-user fees
- per-participant fees
- implementation
- onboarding
- data migration
- integrations
- additional modules
- training
- storage
- support
- future upgrades

It is also worth considering the internal cost of operating the system.

A cheaper platform can become expensive if staff spend significant time:

- entering the same information multiple times
- exporting spreadsheets
- manually reconciling data
- moving between systems
- correcting avoidable errors

When comparing NDIS software, look at the total operational cost rather than subscription price alone.

## A simple NDIS software comparison checklist

Before making a final decision, ask whether the platform can demonstrate the following using your organisation's actual workflows:

- Participant intake and records
- Service agreements and funding
- Rostering and workforce management
- Progress notes and documentation
- Incident management
- Timesheets
- Payroll workflow
- Invoicing
- NDIS claiming
- Reconciliation
- Compliance evidence
- Reporting
- User permissions
- Data migration
- Implementation and training

If possible, involve people from different parts of the organisation in the evaluation.

Operations may notice problems finance does not.

Support workers may identify usability issues management misses.

Compliance teams may ask questions that were not considered during the initial demonstration.

## All-in-one platform or multiple systems?

There is no universal answer.

Some providers prefer separate specialist systems for areas such as:

- rostering
- payroll
- accounting
- participant management
- compliance

Others prefer a more connected environment where operational information can move through the organisation with fewer handovers.

The key question is not whether one approach is automatically better.

It is:

**How much work is required to keep all of your systems connected?**

If your team constantly needs to export, import, reconcile or manually re-enter information, it may be worth reviewing whether the current setup still makes sense.

## Small NDIS provider vs growing organisation

The right software will also depend on your size and stage.

A smaller provider may prioritise:

- simplicity
- affordable pricing
- participant records
- basic rostering
- progress notes
- incidents
- invoicing
- easy onboarding

A growing organisation may increasingly require:

- approval workflows
- stronger workforce controls
- multiple teams or locations
- role-based access
- advanced reporting
- integrations
- automated workflows
- deeper audit trails
- greater operational visibility

Do not buy unnecessary complexity.

But also consider whether the system can continue supporting the organisation as requirements change.

## How TesseractApps approaches NDIS operations

TesseractApps is designed around connected provider workflows.

Rather than treating participant management, workforce operations, service delivery, documentation, finance and reporting as completely separate activities, the platform is designed to connect information across the operational journey.

For organisations comparing NDIS software, the important question is still not how many features are available.

It is whether those capabilities fit the way your organisation actually works.

Before making a decision, map your real workflows and ask every provider—including TesseractApps—to demonstrate them.

## The final question to ask

After every NDIS software demonstration, ask your team:

**“Did this platform actually make our work simpler?”**

A long feature list can look impressive.

But if staff still need spreadsheets, duplicate data entry and multiple disconnected processes to complete everyday work, the underlying problem may remain.

The best NDIS software for your organisation is the platform that fits your current operations, gives you appropriate visibility and can continue supporting you as the organisation develops.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What should I compare when choosing NDIS software?

Compare the complete operational workflow, including participant management, rostering, documentation, workforce management, invoicing, claiming, compliance, reporting, security, implementation and total cost.

### What is the best NDIS software in Australia?

There is no single platform that is best for every provider. The right choice depends on your organisation's size, service model, workforce, operational complexity, existing systems and future requirements.

### Should small NDIS providers use an all-in-one platform?

Not necessarily. Small providers should focus first on the operational problems they genuinely need to solve. However, it is worth considering whether the system can support the organisation if participant numbers, employees and compliance requirements increase.

### How should I test NDIS software before buying?

Use real scenarios from your organisation. Ask the provider to demonstrate a complete workflow rather than only showing dashboards and individual features.

### What questions should I ask during an NDIS software demo?

Ask about real workflows, data migration, participant information, rostering, documentation, incidents, invoicing, claiming, reporting, security, user permissions, implementation, integrations, support and total cost.

# NDIS Software in Australia: What Providers Should Look for in 2026

Learn what providers should compare across rostering, participant management, compliance, claiming, reporting and workforce management.

Running an NDIS provider organisation involves much more than scheduling support workers.

Participant information, service agreements, funding, rosters, case notes, incidents, staff compliance, timesheets, payroll, invoicing, claims and reporting can all become part of the same operational chain.

The problem begins when each part of that chain lives somewhere different.

One system holds the roster. Another handles payroll. Participant documents are stored elsewhere. Finance uses another platform. Compliance evidence sits in folders or spreadsheets.

For smaller providers, this can feel manageable at first.

As the organisation grows, the gaps between those systems can create more administration, duplicate data entry and less visibility over what is happening across the organisation.

That is why choosing NDIS software should not start with a list of features.

It should start with one question:

**How does information move through your organisation from participant intake to service delivery, payment, reporting and audit evidence?**

## What is NDIS software?

NDIS software is technology designed to help disability-service providers manage operational and administrative processes associated with delivering NDIS-funded services.

Depending on the platform, this can include:

- participant management
- service agreements
- funding and budget information
- workforce management
- rostering
- staff availability
- case notes and progress notes
- incident management
- timesheets
- payroll workflows
- invoicing
- NDIS claiming
- compliance records
- reporting
- document management

Not every provider needs every capability from day one.

A five-person provider has very different operational requirements from an organisation with multiple locations and more than 100 employees.

Good software should therefore solve the problems the organisation has now without forcing it to rebuild its systems every time it grows.

## 1. Participant and service information

A participant record should do more than store a name and contact details.

Providers may need to manage information relating to:

- support needs
- risks
- goals
- service agreements
- funding
- documents
- contacts
- delivered services
- incidents
- progress documentation

The key question is whether this information stays connected as the participant moves through different parts of the organisation.

If teams continually copy the same information between separate systems, the administrative burden grows quickly.

## 2. Rostering and workforce management

For providers employing support workers, rostering is often at the centre of daily operations.

When reviewing NDIS rostering software, consider whether your team can see:

- worker availability
- participant requirements
- worker qualifications
- roster conflicts
- shift changes
- cancellations
- completed shifts
- timesheets
- relevant workforce information

For organisations covered by the SCHADS Award, workforce processes can become even more complex.

The goal should not simply be to build a roster.

The goal should be to connect the roster with the rest of the operating process.

## 3. Documentation and incidents

Case notes, progress notes and incident records should not become isolated pieces of information.

Management needs to be able to understand what happened, when it happened, what actions followed and who was responsible.

This becomes particularly important when information is required later for:

- internal review
- participant communication
- reporting
- quality management
- complaints
- audits

A useful NDIS system should make records easier to locate and follow over time.

## 4. Invoicing and claiming

Another area worth testing carefully is what happens after a service is delivered.

Ask:

**Can information move cleanly from the delivered shift or service into the billing and claiming process?**

The more manual re-entry required between service delivery, timesheets, invoicing, claims and reconciliation, the more opportunities there are for discrepancies.

Providers should therefore test the complete workflow rather than looking only at whether a platform has an "invoicing" button.

## 5. Compliance and audit evidence

Software itself does not make an organisation compliant.

Providers still need appropriate policies, people, controls, training and governance.

Technology can, however, make it easier to maintain structured records and see whether important operational requirements have been completed.

When reviewing software, ask whether you can easily answer questions such as:

- Who completed this action?
- When was it completed?
- What changed?
- Who approved it?
- Is a required document missing?
- Is a worker credential approaching expiry?
- Can we retrieve the evidence later?

That is more meaningful than a general claim that a system is "compliance ready".

## 6. Reporting and operational visibility

As organisations grow, managers need more than records.

They need visibility.

That may include understanding:

- workforce utilisation
- service delivery
- incidents
- outstanding actions
- participant funding
- claims
- operational exceptions
- organisational performance

The right information should be available without multiple teams manually rebuilding reports every time management asks a question.

## 7. Security and access

NDIS providers manage sensitive participant and workforce information.

Security therefore needs to be part of the buying decision.

Questions to ask include:

- Where is our data stored?
- Who can access participant information?
- Can access differ by role?
- Are actions logged?
- How is data backed up?
- What happens when an employee leaves?
- Can data be exported if we leave the platform?

Security should be discussed during the software evaluation process, not after implementation.

## NDIS software for small providers vs growing providers

There is no single configuration that suits every organisation.

### Smaller providers may prioritise:

- simple participant records
- rostering
- staff documents
- progress notes
- incidents
- invoicing and claiming
- affordable pricing
- straightforward implementation

### Growing providers may increasingly require:

- approval workflows
- workforce controls
- real-time reporting
- automation
- payroll integration
- multi-site visibility
- stronger governance
- role-based permissions
- deeper audit trails

This is why providers should consider not only what they need today, but what the organisation may require over the next few years.

## How should you compare NDIS software?

Before booking demonstrations, map one real workflow.

For example:

**Participant referral → service agreement → funding → roster → shift → progress note → timesheet → invoice → claim → payment → reporting**

Then ask every software provider to show you how that workflow operates.

Don't let the demonstration stay on the dashboard.

Test the actual work your team performs.

## Where TesseractApps fits

TesseractApps has been designed around a connected NDIS operating flow rather than treating each activity as an isolated tool.

The current platform maps operations from participant intake and service agreements through funding, rostering, shift delivery, documentation, incidents, timesheets, payroll, invoicing, claiming, reconciliation, reporting and audit evidence.

The platform also uses a provider-maturity approach, where configuration and governance depth can develop as an organisation grows rather than requiring providers to move onto an entirely separate product.

For providers comparing systems, however, the same principle still applies:

**Don't choose software because the feature list looks long. Choose it because the workflows fit the way your organisation actually operates.**

## Before choosing your next NDIS platform

Ask three questions:

1. Does it solve our current operational problems?
2. Can our information move between different parts of the organisation without constant manual re-entry?
3. Will the system still make sense if we grow?

Those answers will tell you much more than the number of features on a pricing page.



## FAQ

### What software do NDIS providers use?

Providers use different combinations of participant management, rostering, workforce, finance, documentation and compliance systems. Some organisations choose separate tools while others use a more connected provider-management platform.

### Do small NDIS providers need software?

Not every small provider needs a complex platform. However, as participant numbers, employees and documentation requirements grow, structured software can reduce reliance on disconnected spreadsheets and manual processes.

### What should NDIS software include?

The answer depends on the provider model, but common areas include participant management, rostering, workforce records, documentation, incidents, invoicing, claiming, reporting and compliance records.

### How do I choose NDIS software?

Map your most important real-world workflows and ask each vendor to demonstrate them from beginning to end. Compare usability, implementation, security, data migration, support and total cost as well as features.

# Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 for SCHADS Employers: Your EOFY Survival Guide

How SCHADS-covered AU disability employers should finalise STP Phase 2, categorise allowances correctly, and handle termination payments at EOFY.

Single Touch Payroll Phase 2 is now the permanent reporting standard for Australian employers, with no further extensions or transition deferrals. For most industries, that's a settled fact of payroll life. For [SCHADS-covered disability employers](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers), STP Phase 2 is a genuinely harder standard to meet, because the award's allowance structure, casual-heavy workforce and high staff turnover all interact directly with the parts of the reporting standard that trip employers up most: allowance categorisation and termination reporting.

This guide walks Payroll Managers through STP Phase 2 for SCHADS employers specifically, why the two categories above cause more errors here than in other sectors, and why getting them wrong at EOFY now carries a bigger downstream cost than it used to.

## What disaggregation of gross actually requires?

STP Phase 2 replaced the old single "gross" figure with a requirement to separately report each component of an employee's pay: paid leave, allowances, [overtime](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates), bonuses and commissions, director's fees, salary sacrifice, and lump sum payments. The ATO calls this the disaggregation of gross, and the purpose isn't just tidier reporting. This richer data feeds employee income statements, pre-fills tax returns, and flows through to Services Australia in real time for employees with a Centrelink customer reference number, so an incorrectly classified payment doesn't just sit quietly in your payroll system. It can misstate an employee's assessable income for Family Tax Benefit or child support purposes, and it's exactly the kind of error that can hold up your STP finalisation with the ATO.

For a SCHADS employer, this matters more than for most industries because the award itself generates a long list of allowance types across a single roster: travel, transport and fares, sleepover, laundry and uniform, first aid, leading hand or supervisory duties, broken shift, on-call and recall, and higher duties or qualification-based allowances. Each one needs to be mapped to the correct ATO allowance category, not bundled together. A generic retail or hospitality payroll setup rarely has to solve this many allowance types for a single employee, which is exactly why STP Phase 2 catches out disability employers more than most.

## Where SCHADS allowances go wrong in STP Phase 2?

The ATO has specifically flagged incorrect use of the "Other allowances" category as one of the most common STP Phase 2 mistakes. It's also one of the easiest mistakes for a SCHADS employer to make, because several award allowances don't map neatly onto a single obvious ATO category.

A few practical points worth checking against your own configuration:

- Travel and transport allowances generally fall under specific ATO categories such as award transport payments or cents-per-kilometre allowances, not a generic catch-all. Confirm which applies based on how the allowance is actually calculated and paid, since the two are treated differently for withholding purposes.
- Qualification and higher duties allowances typically have their own reporting category rather than sitting in "Other allowances." Getting this wrong doesn't just misreport the payment, it can affect how the ATO's pre-fill logic treats the employee's deduction eligibility.
- All-purpose allowances that form part of overtime are an exception to standard allowance reporting. If an allowance is folded into a rate that then attracts overtime, the ATO requires it to be reported as overtime, not as a separate allowance, because overtime is treated differently for superannuation guarantee purposes.
- Cashed-out leave and unused leave on termination are also exceptions. Amounts paid as cashing out leave in service, or as unused leave on termination, are reported under the relevant leave type, not as an allowance, even where an allowance rate was used to calculate the payment.

Given how many SCHADS employees move between ordinary hours, overtime, [sleepover ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel)shifts and [broken shifts](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches) within a single pay cycle, a payroll configuration built once and left unreviewed is the most common source of these errors, not a one-off data entry mistake.

## Termination payments: where high turnover meets high complexity?

Disability and community services has one of the [highest staff turnover](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/hidden-costs-workforce-management) rates of any SCHADS-covered sector, and STP Phase 2 introduced several new payment classifications specifically for termination that many payroll configurations still don't handle correctly.

- Leave, unused leave on termination is its own classification, separate from standard leave categories, introduced specifically for Phase 2 reporting.
- Lump Sum A splits into two types depending on the reason for termination and when the leave accrued: Type R for genuine redundancy, invalidity or early retirement, and Type T for normal termination. Reporting the wrong type doesn't just misreport the payment; it can misstate how much of it is taxed concessionally.
- Lump Sum D covers the tax-free component of a genuine redundancy or approved early retirement payment and must be reported even where it's the only amount paid to that employee in the financial year, a requirement that didn't exist under STP Phase 1.
- ETP codes distinguish life benefit from death benefit payments and the reason for payment. Getting the wrong code assigned affects how the ATO calculates the employee's tax treatment on that payment.
- Cessation reason codes must be reported for every termination, using the ATO's standard set of codes. For a workforce with a high proportion of fixed-term, casual and contract-ending roles, as most SCHADS employers do, this is worth a specific check rather than a default code applied to every exit.

At EOFY specifically, this is where finalisation most often stalls. If a termination processed earlier in the year used the wrong lump sum type or cessation reason, that error carries through to the employee's income statement and can hold up your STP finalisation declaration while it's corrected.

## Why this now affects more than your STP finalisation?

From 1 July 2026, Payday Super requires the Superannuation Guarantee to be paid on the same timeline as wages, and enforcement of that obligation depends directly on the disaggregated data reported through STP Phase 2. If your payroll system incorrectly includes unused leave on termination in the super guarantee calculation base, for example, it will over-report the super liability for that pay event. That's not a shortfall the ATO will chase you for, but it creates a reconciliation discrepancy that can trigger a data-matching enquiry, precisely the kind of thing an EOFY reconciliation should catch before it becomes an external question.

In other words, allowance and termination misclassifications that used to be a tidiness issue inside your own payroll system are now data quality issues the ATO cross-checks against your super payments in near real time.

## Your EOFY checklist for STP Phase 2 as a SCHADS employer

- Audit your [allowance mapping](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-audit-guide-self-assess-fair-work) against the full list of SCHADS allowance types your organisation actually pays, not just the most common ones, and confirm none are defaulting to "Other allowances."
- Check overtime-linked all-purpose allowances are reported as overtime, not as a separate allowance category, for every role where this applies.
- Review every termination processed this financial year for correct lump sum type, ETP code and cessation reason before lodging your STP finalisation declaration.
- Confirm unused leave on termination is excluded from your super guarantee calculation base where it should be, to avoid over-reporting liability that creates a reconciliation gap.
- Treat this as an ongoing configuration review, not an annual one. New allowance types, new award clauses and new termination scenarios appear throughout the year, and Payday Super means data quality issues now surface every pay cycle, not just at EOFY.

## Frequently asked questions

Is STP Phase 2 still being phased in, or is it now compulsory? It's fully compulsory. There are no further extensions or transition deferrals, and every pay run must include disaggregated payment information reported directly to the ATO.

What's the most common STP Phase 2 mistake for disability employers specifically? Defaulting SCHADS allowances, particularly travel, qualification and higher duties allowances, into the generic "Other allowances" category instead of their specific ATO classification. The ATO has flagged this as one of the most common reporting errors across all industries, and disability employers are more exposed to it than most simply because the award generates more allowance types per employee.

Does payroll EOFY 2026 change anything about how terminations are reported? The termination reporting rules themselves, lump sum types, ETP codes, cessation reasons, haven't changed for this EOFY. What has changed is the consequence of getting them wrong: from 1 July 2026, Payday Super enforcement relies on the same disaggregated data, so a termination misclassification can now surface as a superannuation reconciliation issue, not just a tax reporting one.

Do we need to fix historical STP Phase 2 misclassifications, or just get this year right? Fixing this year's finalisation is the immediate priority, but a misclassification that's been repeating pay cycle after pay cycle is worth correcting at the configuration level, not just patching the current year's data. Otherwise the same error reappears at your next ATO STP finalisation.

## Get your STP Phase 2 configuration checked before you finalise

Reviewing allowance mapping and termination reporting across a full year of SCHADS payroll isn't a job for a manual spot-check the week before your STP finalisation is due. For the broader FY2025-26 close-out process this fits into, see our [EOFY checklist](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/eofy-checklist-for-ndis-providers-tax-bas-reporting-made-simple), and if you want a second set of eyes on your current payroll configuration specifically, book a payroll demo and we'll walk through your allowance categories and termination reporting against what the ATO actually expects.

Payroll configuration can be reviewed alongside your EOFY close-out so the same reporting issue does not repeat into the next financial year.

# EOFY Checklist for NDIS Providers: Tax, BAS & Reporting Made Simple

A step-by-step EOFY guide for Australian NDIS providers covering STP finalisation, BAS, super guarantee reconciliation, NDIS claim reconciliation.

End of financial year lands at an awkward time for NDIS providers. It is the same window as the new NDIS Pricing Schedule taking effect, [SCHADS Award rate changes](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers) flowing through payroll, and the usual STP finalisation, BAS and superannuation obligations every employer faces. None of these processes are optional, and several depend on each other: your STP finalisation only reconciles cleanly if your payroll data is correct, and your payroll data is only correct if your award rates and NDIS claim rates were updated on time.

That is what makes EOFY for NDIS providers a genuinely different task to a standard close-out, and why a generic checklist usually leaves gaps. This checklist works through each obligation in order, with the specific dates, rates and thresholds that apply for the FY2025-26 close-out, so your finance team can work through it once rather than chasing each requirement separately.

**Key FY2025-26 dates at a glance**

- **Q4 super guarantee payment:** 28 July
- **STP finalisation (arms-length employees):** 14 July
- **Payroll tax annual reconciliation:** Around 21 July (confirm your state)
- **Monthly BAS (with registered agent extension):** Varies by lodgment program tier

## 1. Single Touch Payroll finalisation

STP finalisation is the declaration confirming your payroll reporting for the financial year is complete for every employee. Until it is lodged, employees see "not tax ready" in myGov and cannot accurately lodge their own returns.

- **Deadline:** 14 July, for arms-length employees. Closely held payees, such as family members of a director, may have a later due date, so check this separately rather than applying one deadline to your whole workforce.
- **Before you finalise:** Confirm you are finalising the correct financial year, that you have reported under the right ABN throughout, and that if you changed payroll software or employee payroll IDs during the year, those changes have been reconciled rather than left as duplicate or orphaned records.
- **Fringe benefits:** If you provided any fringe benefits during the FBT year (1 April to 31 March), the reportable fringe benefits amount needs to be included through STP as part of finalisation, not lodged separately.
- **STP Phase 2 detail:** Confirm income types are correctly disaggregated: salary, overtime, bonuses, leave and commissions reported separately rather than bundled, along with employment basis and cessation reason for any employee who left during the year. Errors here are a common reason finalisation gets rejected or queried.

For a disability provider running a large casual and part-time SCHADS-covered workforce, EOFY payroll for disability services is also the point where sleepover, [broken shift ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches)and [penalty rate](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates) misclassifications from earlier in the year surface. If your STP totals look wrong for a pay category, check it against the award rules that actually applied on those pay dates before finalising, not after.

## 2. Superannuation guarantee reconciliation

The Superannuation Guarantee rate for FY2025-26 is 12%, up from 11.5% the previous year, and this is the final scheduled increase under the legislated timetable. It applies to all wages paid on or after 1 July 2025, even where part of the pay period falls before that date.

- **Concessional contributions cap:** $30,000 for FY2025-26, up from $27,500. This includes employer SG contributions and any salary sacrifice, relevant if you are advising employees or checking your own contribution strategy.
- **Maximum contribution base:** $62,500 per quarter for FY2025-26. Super is not payable on earnings above this cap in a given quarter, which matters for higher-paid clinical or management roles.
- **Missed or late payments:** The super guarantee charge applies if contributions are late or short, carrying 10% annual interest plus a $20 administration fee per employee. Unlike an on-time SG payment, a late SGC payment is not tax deductible. If you find a shortfall during EOFY reconciliation, lodge a Superannuation Guarantee Charge Statement and pay it promptly rather than folding it quietly into next quarter's payment.

**A structural change to flag now, not just at EOFY:** Payday Super began on 1 July 2026, requiring SG to be paid at the same time as wages rather than quarterly. The Small Business Superannuation Clearing House also closed permanently to all users from that date. If your payroll process still assumes a quarterly super cycle, this needs to be corrected as a process change, not an EOFY line item, since it affects every pay run going forward, not just your FY2025-26 close-out.

## 3. BAS and GST reconciliation

BAS for an NDIS provider carries one wrinkle most generic small business guidance skips: most support items are GST-free, but not all provider income is, so getting this wrong in either direction is common. Whether you lodge monthly or quarterly, EOFY is the point to check your full-year BAS position rather than just lodging the final period in isolation.

- **Reconcile GST collected and claimed** for the full year against your general ledger, checking specifically for any NDIS-related supply that was coded incorrectly.
- **Match PAYG withholding** reported through STP against what was actually remitted to the ATO across the year, catching any timing mismatches before they show up as a discrepancy at tax return time.
- **Check your lodgment program dates.** Monthly BAS reporters using a registered agent typically get a short extension beyond the standard 21st of the month deadline, but the exact extension depends on your agent's lodgment program tier, so confirm the specific date with your agent rather than assuming a standard extension applies.

## 4. Payroll tax reconciliation

If your total Australian wages exceed your state's payroll tax threshold, an annual reconciliation is due to your state revenue office, separate from your BAS and STP obligations.

- Confirm actual wages match what was declared in your periodic returns across the year.
- Most states set the annual reconciliation due date around 21 July, but this varies, so check your specific state's date rather than assuming national consistency.
- If you operate across multiple states, which is common for larger NDIS providers, work through each state's threshold and wage base separately rather than one combined total.

## 5. NDIS-specific claim reconciliation

This is the step that is easy to miss if your EOFY checklist was built for a generic services business rather than an NDIS provider specifically.

- **Reconcile claims against the NDIS portal,** not just your own billing system, to catch any [claims rejected or adjusted](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/ndis-bulk-payment-claim-rejections) by the Agency during the year that did not flow back into your internal records.
- **Check the [1 July pricing transition ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/ndis-pricing-arrangements-2026-27-what-changed)specifically.** Any pay period or service delivered either side of 1 July needs to be claimed at the price limits that applied on the actual service date, not the date the claim was processed. This is one of the most common sources of NDIS claim errors precisely because it lands in the same week as several other EOFY processes competing for your team's attention.
- **Confirm [SIL claims](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/ndis-sil-mandatory-registration-2026-checklist/)** used the correct item codes either side of the transition, since SIL item numbers changed prefix this year. A claim using the wrong code is not just a data error; it can be rejected outright.
- **Reconfirm TTP loading eligibility** if your organisation claims it, since ongoing eligibility depends on meeting benchmarking requirements that should be checked annually, not assumed to carry over unchanged.

## 6. Audit-ready records, not just EOFY records

Everything above produces records the [Fair Work Ombudsman](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-audit-guide-self-assess-fair-work), the NDIA or the ATO can request, sometimes years later. Under the Fair Work Act, employee records must be kept for seven years, whether or not your EOFY process currently treats record-keeping as a compliance task or a filing afterthought. Every reconciliation you complete this week creates evidence. How you store it determines whether that evidence works for you or against you.

- Store STP finalisation confirmations, BAS lodgment receipts, super payment confirmations and NDIS claim reconciliation reports together by financial year, not scattered across separate systems.
- Keep a short written record of any correction made during EOFY reconciliation: what was wrong, when it was fixed, and how. This is exactly the evidence that helps if a regulator asks about a specific pay period later.
- Treat this year's reconciliation as the baseline for next year's opening figures, so errors do not compound silently from one financial year into the next.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the STP finalisation deadline for FY2025-26?

14 July, for arms-length employees. Closely held payees, such as directors' family members paid informally, may have a later due date, and this should be checked separately rather than assumed to match the general deadline.

### Do NDIS providers have different EOFY obligations to other employers?

The core obligations, STP, super, BAS and payroll tax, are the same as any employer. What is different is the overlap with NDIS-specific processes landing in the same window: the 1 July Pricing Schedule transition, SCHADS Award rate changes, and claim reconciliation against the NDIA portal, all of which can affect the payroll and revenue figures feeding into your other EOFY reporting.

### What happens if we miss a superannuation guarantee payment?

You need to lodge a Superannuation Guarantee Charge Statement and pay the shortfall, which carries 10% annual interest plus a $20 administration fee per affected employee. Unlike an on-time SG payment, a late SGC payment is not tax deductible, which makes catching a shortfall during EOFY reconciliation rather than at your next external audit worth the extra checking time.

### Does Payday Super affect our FY2025-26 close-out?

Not directly, since it began on 1 July 2026, after the FY2025-26 year closed. It does affect how you process super from that date forward, so it belongs on your EOFY checklist as a forward-looking action item: confirm your payroll system pays SG each payday rather than quarterly, and confirm your super clearing arrangement no longer relies on the Small Business Superannuation Clearing House, which closed permanently from the same date.

## Turn this checklist into a working document

Running STP finalisation, super reconciliation, BAS, payroll tax and NDIS claim reconciliation as five separate processes, each with its own deadline, is where EOFY mistakes happen for disability providers specifically. The dates and thresholds in this checklist are for FY2025-26, and several, including the Superannuation Guarantee rate and the Payday Super transition, carry straight into how you run payroll for FY2026-27 as well.

For the full checklist as a working document your team can tick off item by item, and how it connects to your day-to-day payroll process, download the EOFY checklist and work through it against your own records rather than starting from a blank page.

Tesseractapps connects payroll, rostering and NDIS claiming so your EOFY close-out does not require five separate reconciliation passes. Visit [tesseractapps.com.au](https://tesseractapps.com.au) to see how it works.

# NDIS Price Guide 2026-27 vs 2025-26: Line-by-Line Breakdown of Support Item Changes

Side-by-side comparison of NDIS support item codes and price limits for 2026-27 vs 2025-26

The NDIS Pricing Schedule 2026-27 took effect on 1 July 2026, and against the 2025-26 catalogue, 25 support items were removed and 33 new ones added across a catalogue of 624 current codes. Layered on top of that are rate changes that moved in different directions depending on the support type, plus a handful of structural changes that affect how items are claimed, not just what they cost. For a billing or claims team, checking the new rates is not really the task this year. The task is reconciling your price book item by item against a catalogue that changed shape as well as price, then updating service agreements and claim templates to match.

This is that line-by-line comparison.

## Support worker rates: 2025-26 vs 2026-27

Support worker rates rose approximately 4.8% across the board, reflecting the Fair Work Commission's 2026 [SCHADS Award](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers) decision and the increase in the Superannuation Guarantee to 12%.

**Support worker rate comparison: 2025-26 vs 2026-27**

- **Weekday daytime:** $70.23/hr (2025-26) to $73.58/hr (2026-27)
- **Evening:** proportional increase to $81.07/hr (2026-27)
- **Saturday:** proportional increase to $103.54/hr (2026-27)
- **Sunday:** proportional increase to $133.50/hr (2026-27)
- **Public holiday:** proportional increase to $163.46/hr (2026-27)

The 2025-26 comparison figures for evening, Saturday, Sunday, and public holiday rates are not published as a single confirmed line in publicly available sources. Before updating your price book, pull last year's exact figures from your own records for those categories rather than assuming a flat 4.8% applies uniformly, since penalty rate structures do not always move in perfect lockstep with the base rate.

## Therapy rates: some up, some down, most unchanged

This is where checking every line matters most. The 2026-27 review did not apply a blanket increase to allied health. It benchmarked each discipline separately against Medicare and private health insurance data from more than 16 million therapy claims, and the outcomes varied.

**Allied health rate comparison: 2025-26 vs 2026-27**

- **Psychology:** $232.99/hr to $252.99/hr — up $20.00 (+8.6%)
- **Dietetics:** $188.99/hr to $178.99/hr — down $10.00
- **Exercise physiology:** $166.99/hr to $161.99/hr — down $5.00
- **Occupational therapy:** $193.99/hr — unchanged
- **Speech pathology:** $193.99/hr — unchanged
- **Physiotherapy:** $183.99/hr — unchanged
- **Podiatry:** $188.99/hr — unchanged

Audiology was also held at its 2025-26 rate, though we have not been able to independently confirm its exact dollar figure for this comparison. Check it against the published Pricing Schedule directly rather than assuming it moved with the rest of the frozen group. Psychology was the only therapy discipline to receive an increase this review.

**Nursing rates: 2025-26 vs 2026-27**

- **Enrolled nurse:** $99.88/hr to $103.44/hr
- **Registered nurse:** $123.65/hr to $128.05/hr
- **Clinical nurse:** $143.04/hr to $148.13/hr
- **Nurse practitioner:** $176.85/hr to $183.15/hr

All four nursing levels rose by approximately 3.6%, in line with the broader wage-related cost increases flowing through this year's schedule. If your billing system applies a flat percentage adjustment across all therapy line items, that will overpay on dietetics and exercise physiology and underpay on psychology, in both cases producing a claim that does not match the Pricing Schedule.

## Support coordination and plan management: mostly frozen

Support coordination rates were not increased for 2026-27, and providers have raised this as a point of ongoing concern given rates have not moved since 2019-20.

- **Support Coordination Level 1:** $80.06/hr — unchanged
- **Support Coordination Level 2:** $100.14/hr — unchanged
- **Support Coordination Level 3:** $190.54/hr — unchanged
- **Plan management monthly fee (14_034_0127_8_3):** $104.45/month — unchanged

The plan management monthly fee itself is unchanged, but a related line item has been removed entirely. The separate plan management establishment or set-up fee no longer appears in the 2026-27 schedule. If a plan-managed participant is billed a set-up fee this year, that is worth querying against the current catalogue rather than assuming it is still a valid claimable item.

## Structural changes that are not about price at all

Several of this year's biggest practical changes for billing and claims teams do not show up as a rate movement at all. They show up as new item numbers and restructured claim types.

### Therapy items split into six line items per discipline

The old single claim type system for allied health has been replaced. Each therapy discipline now has separate item numbers for direct service, cancellation, non-face-to-face support, provider travel, NDIA-requested reports, and telehealth. Telehealth did not exist as a standalone item in 2025-26; it is new and separately claimable in 2026-27. If your billing templates still reference last year's single item number per discipline, they will need to be rebuilt against the new structure, not just re-priced.

### Short Term Accommodation has been restructured

STA now includes separate line items for participant accommodation and support worker accommodation, rather than one combined item. This affects how STA claims should be itemised going forward.

### SIL has a new registration group and item prefix

[Supported Independent Living](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/ndis-sil-mandatory-registration-2026-checklist) items now carry a 0138 prefix in place of the previous 0115, alongside the roughly 4.8% rate increase applied to SIL supports. For claims spanning the 1 July transition, supports delivered before that date use the old 0115 codes, and supports delivered on or after it use the new 0138 codes.

### Provider travel for therapy stays capped at 50% of the hourly rate

This rule is not new for 2026-27; it carried over from the 2025-26 schedule. It is easy to overlook when reconciling therapy line items against the new six-item structure, so it is worth confirming your billing system still applies it correctly under the new item numbers.

## The bigger structural shift behind this year's changes

Two things are worth understanding beyond the individual line items. First, the NDIA has stopped calling these figures price limits and now frames them as appropriate and reasonable maximum prices, language introduced ahead of a proposed Ministerial power to make binding pricing determinations under the National Disability Insurance Scheme Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Bill 2026, introduced into Parliament in May 2026. Second, the claiming rules and updated Support Catalogue that would normally accompany the Pricing Schedule have not been republished yet. The price tables are confirmed and in effect; the detailed rules for edge cases still sit with last year's guidance until the NDIA releases an update.

Neither of these is a reason to delay updating your price book. Both are reasons to keep checking the NDIA's pricing page for updates rather than treating 1 July as the final word on 2026-27.

There is also a change coming that sits just outside this comparison but is worth flagging now: from 1 January 2027, participants using an unregistered provider for community access supports will see the claimable rate reduced. It does not affect your 2026-27 price book today, but if your service works with self-managed participants and unregistered arrangements, it is worth building into your next planning cycle rather than treating it as a surprise in six months.

## What billing and claims teams should reconcile this week

- **Rebuild therapy item templates** around the new six-line-item structure per discipline, including the new standalone telehealth items, rather than re-pricing the old single item numbers.
- **Check every therapy discipline individually.** Psychology rose, dietetics and exercise physiology fell, occupational therapy, speech pathology, and physiotherapy stayed flat, and podiatry, audiology, and nursing need their exact figures confirmed against the published schedule. A single blanket adjustment will get most of these wrong.
- **Remove the plan management set-up fee** from any active billing templates if it is still configured as claimable.
- **Split SIL claims at 1 July,** using 0115 codes before the effective date and 0138 codes from it, with the roughly 4.8% rate increase applied only to the new codes.
- **Re-itemise Short Term Accommodation claims** into participant accommodation and support worker accommodation components going forward.
- **Confirm evening, Saturday, Sunday, and public holiday support worker rates** against your own 2025-26 records rather than assuming a uniform 4.8% uplift across every time category.

## Get the full comparison in one place

Reconciling 25 removed items, 33 new items, and rate changes running in different directions across a 624-item catalogue is not a task you want to run from memory or a stack of separate PDFs. For the full support worker rate breakdown by category and how it flows into your invoicing, see our billing hub or visit our July pricing pillar for ongoing updates as the NDIA finalises the remaining 2026-27 rules documents.

Want the changes in one place? Get the cheat sheet and update your price book in one pass. Visit [tesseractapps.com.au](https://tesseractapps.com.au) to access the full rate comparison and billing hub.
