# NDIS Pricing Arrangements 2026-27: What's Changed and What It Means for Your Provider?

A breakdown of the NDIS Pricing Schedule 2026-27: check what Finance and Service Managers must update before the next billing cycle.

The National Disability Insurance Agency released the results of its 2026-27 Annual Pricing Review on 22 June 2026, with these price changes taking effect from 1 July 2026. If your service agreements, billing system, or payroll still reference last financial year's figures, every invoice you raise from that date carries a small but real risk of over-claiming or under-claiming.

This year's update is bigger than a straightforward rate adjustment. Alongside the annual price changes, the NDIA restructured how it publishes pricing information, changed how Supported Independent Living is registered and coded, and began phasing down a loading some providers have relied on for years. Here is what actually changed, what is still only proposed, and what Finance and Service Managers need to update before the next billing cycle.

## The 2026-27 NDIS Pricing Arrangements at a glance

- **Effective date:** 1 July 2026 (released 22 June 2026)
- **Support worker weekday daytime rate:** $70.23 to $73.58 per hour
- **Plan management fee:** unchanged at $104.45 per month
- **SIL support items:** recoded from 0115 to 0138 from 1 July 2026
- **Publishing format:** one combined PAPL document replaced by three separate publications
- **TTP loading:** being phased down, subject to benchmarking requirements

## The publishing structure has changed too

In previous years, everything sat in one combined document, the NDIS Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits, commonly shortened to PAPL and still often called the NDIS price guide out of habit even though that is no longer the NDIA's official name for it. For 2026-27, that single document has been split into three separate publications:

- **The Annual Pricing Review,** which sets out the evidence and reasoning behind the year's pricing decisions.
- **The NDIS Pricing Schedule,** which lists support item numbers, names, units, and the maximum national, remote, and very remote prices effective from 1 July 2026.
- **The NDIS Support Catalogue,** which sits alongside the Pricing Schedule as the reference for support item structure.

Worth flagging for your compliance team: the NDIA has published the price tables, but not yet a full rules document covering claiming, travel, cancellation, and non-face-to-face provisions in the same detail the old PAPL provided. If your billing system relies on those rules for edge cases, check current guidance with your software provider or the NDIA rather than assuming last year's rules still apply in full.

## What actually changed in the rates?

Rate increases largely flow from two sources: the Fair Work Commission's 2026 SCHADS Award decision and the increase in the Superannuation Guarantee, both of which push up the cost of delivering support.

### Support worker rates rose

The standard weekday daytime rate for core supports moved from $70.23 to $73.58 per hour, roughly a 4.8% increase, with proportional increases carried through evening, night, weekend, and public holiday rates. If your price book or invoicing templates still show last year's figures, this is the first thing to update.

### Therapy rates moved in different directions

The NDIA compared NDIS prices against Medicare and private health insurance data across more than 16 million therapy claims, and the results were not uniform:

- **Psychology rates rose** from $232.99 to $252.99 per hour, reflecting that NDIS rates were sitting below what Medicare and private health funds pay. This change is intended to make it easier for participants to access psychologists.
- **Dietetics rates fell** from $188.99 to $178.99 per hour, because NDIS rates were assessed as higher than the Medicare and private health fund comparison.
- **Exercise physiology rates were also adjusted down,** having been assessed as above the Medicare comparison benchmark.

If your service delivers a mix of these supports, do not assume every line item moved in the same direction. Check each support item individually against the new Pricing Schedule rather than applying a flat percentage increase across your whole price book.

### Some fees stayed flat

The monthly plan management fee is confirmed unchanged at $104.45 (item 14_034_0127_8_3). The NDIA has flagged a review of whether a flat monthly fee still makes sense as the sector changes, so treat this as stable for now rather than permanently fixed.

## Item code and registration changes: the NDIS support item updates to check first

The most operationally significant structural change is in Supported Independent Living. A new registration group has been introduced for SIL, and the associated support items now carry a 0138 prefix in place of the previous 0115.

This is not just a renumbering exercise for your records. For SIL supports delivered before 1 July 2026, continue claiming under the existing 0115 codes. For supports delivered on or after that date, use the new 0138 item numbers. Get this wrong and claims can be rejected or, worse, processed incorrectly against the wrong registration group. If SIL is a meaningful part of your service mix, this should be the first thing your billing team checks against the new Support Catalogue.

## A remote loading change still in the pipeline

Not everything in the 2026-27 Annual Pricing Review is locked in yet. The NDIA has proposed two new isolated town classifications, with Type 1 Isolated Towns treated as MM6 for remote price loadings and travel arrangements, but this is currently a recommendation, not a confirmed price, and sits outside the Pricing Schedule that took effect on 1 July 2026. If your service operates in or near a regional area, track this specifically rather than assuming your current remoteness classification carries forward unchanged. Only figures in the published Pricing Schedule are safe to build into your billing system today.

## The TTP loading is being phased down

Providers claiming the Temporary Transformation Payment loading need to check their continued eligibility. The loading is being phased down under the 2026-27 arrangements, and providers must still meet the underlying benchmarking requirements to claim it. Claiming TTP without meeting those requirements is treated as a compliance breach, not just an overpayment to be corrected later, so this is worth a direct conversation with your finance team rather than an assumption that last year's eligibility still applies.

## The mid-year claiming trap

Here is where a lot of providers get caught out every year, and 2026-27 is no exception. A single fortnightly pay period can straddle 30 June and 1 July. Supports delivered before the effective date must be claimed at the old price limits, and supports delivered on or after it use the new limits, regardless of when the pay run or invoice is actually processed.

If your rostering or billing system does not stamp every shift and invoice line with an accurate service date, this is genuinely easy to get wrong at scale, particularly across a large casual workforce delivering shifts every day of the week through the transition period. The fix is not a manual reminder to staff. It is a system that applies the correct price limit automatically based on the actual date the support was delivered, not the date it happens to be processed.

## Frequently asked questions

### When did the NDIS Pricing Arrangements 2026-27 take effect?

From 1 July 2026, following the Annual Pricing Review results released by the NDIA on 22 June 2026.

### Is the NDIS Price Guide the same thing as the NDIS Pricing Schedule?

Functionally, yes. The NDIA has moved away from the combined PAPL document many providers still call the price guide, replacing it with the NDIS Pricing Schedule as the source for maximum prices, alongside separate Annual Pricing Review and Support Catalogue publications.

### Do I need to update my service agreements immediately?

Yes, and you need to speak with each participant before applying new rates, regardless of whether they are agency managed, plan managed, or self managed. Update billing systems and service agreements together rather than treating them as separate tasks.

### What happens to invoices for shifts that straddle 30 June and 1 July?

Supports delivered before 1 July are claimed at the old price limits, and supports delivered on or after that date use the new limits, based on the actual service date, not the date the invoice is processed.

## What to update before your next billing cycle

- **Service agreements.** Under the new arrangements, providers must speak with participants before changing service agreement rates, whether the participant is agency managed, plan managed, or self managed. Build this conversation into your update timeline, not just your billing system update.
- **Billing and invoicing systems.** Update price books against the new Pricing Schedule item by item, not with a blanket percentage adjustment, given rates moved in different directions across support types.
- **Payroll.** Confirm support worker pay rates and on-costs align with the SCHADS changes underpinning the new price limits, so your margin assumptions hold up once the new prices are in effect.
- **SIL claims specifically.** Confirm your team is using 0115 codes for supports delivered before 1 July 2026 and 0138 codes from that date, with no gap or overlap in your claiming records.
- **TTP eligibility.** Reconfirm benchmarking requirements are still met before continuing to claim the loading.
- **Historical claims audit.** Spot-check invoices raised either side of 1 July for pay periods that straddled the transition, to catch mid-year claiming errors early rather than at your next NDIA compliance check.

## Get ahead of the next update

NDIS pricing changes every year, and the 2026-27 arrangements have brought a bigger structural shift than most, from the SIL registration restructure to the split into three separate publications. Providers that update service agreements, billing systems, and payroll item by item, rather than assuming a flat increase, are the ones that avoid rejected claims and awkward retrospective corrections at audit time.

For the full item-by-item breakdown and ongoing updates as the remaining 2026-27 rules documents are released, visit our pricing updates hub, check how it flows through to your billing setup, and review your service agreements against the new requirements.

Want the changes in one place? Download the Price Change Cheat Sheet and update your price book in one pass instead of hunting through the new Pricing Schedule line by line.

---

# Top 7 SCHADS Award Breaches Found by Fair Work, and How Software Prevents Them

The seven SCHADS breaches Fair Work most often penalises Australian providers for, with real case examples, and the automated controls that stop them at source.

The Fair Work Ombudsman has made disability and aged care a priority enforcement area, and the numbers back it up. In the 2024 to 2025 financial year alone, the regulator recovered more than $30 million in underpayments from the care sector. Since January 2025, intentional underpayment is also a criminal offence: companies face the greater of $7.825 million or three times the underpayment amount, and individuals found guilty face up to 10 years' imprisonment.

None of that is meant to alarm you. Most SCHADS breaches at NDIS and disability providers are not deliberate. They come from award interpretation errors, spreadsheets that cannot keep up with more than 3,000 possible pay rate combinations, and payroll systems that were not built for a modern award this complex. Below are the seven SCHADS award breaches Fair Work most consistently finds, with real cases behind each one, and what actually stops them before they reach payroll.

## 1. Sleepover and night shift loading errors

[Sleepovers are the single most litigated area of the SCHADS Award](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel) right now. For years the Fair Work Ombudsman held that work performed either side of a sleepover formed one continuous shift, triggering a 15% night shift loading. That position was tested in Jats Joint Pty Ltd v Fair Work Ombudsman [2025] FCA 743, where the Federal Court found in the employer's favour and ruled that a sleepover does not form part of a shift. The Full Federal Court then dismissed the Ombudsman's appeal in March 2026.

The Fair Work Commission has since settled the question by varying the award itself. From the first full pay period on or after 1 June 2026, sleepovers officially do not count as a break, work either side is treated as one continuous shift, and shift penalties are now calculated separately for each active work period rather than across the whole engagement. Providers running 24-hour care models are now managing three different rule sets depending on the pay period in question: pre-Jats Joint, post-Jats Joint, and post-June 2026 determination.

**How software prevents it:** Rostering and payroll platforms with SCHADS interpretation built in apply the correct sleepover, shift, and penalty logic automatically based on the pay period date, rather than relying on payroll staff to track which legal position applied when.

## 2. Applying the wrong award or classification stream

[SCHADS has four streams and up to eight classification levels](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers), and the gap between them is material. A Level 2 worker in the Home Care and Disability stream and a Level 2 worker in the Social and Community Services stream sit on different base rates entirely. Some providers compound the problem by classifying support workers under the Home Care Award instead of SCHADS altogether, a red flag that industry bodies including the Australian Services Union actively watch for.

Get the stream or level wrong on day one and every subsequent pay run inherits the error, often for years before anyone notices.

**How software prevents it:** Classification logic tied to role, funding stream, and duties, checked at onboarding and flagged automatically if a role looks misclassified against its actual work pattern.

## 3. Missed travel, transport, and fare allowances

The Fair Work Ombudsman issued a Compliance Notice to disability provider Agape in October 2024 after two employees, one casual and one full-time, were found to have been underpaid between November 2023 and May 2024. The alleged underpayments totalled $7,789.42, driven by the casual worker's minimum hourly rate and travelling, transport, and fare allowances under SCHADS, and the full-time worker's annual leave entitlements under the National Employment Standards.

[Travel time and allowances](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately) are a recurring blind spot precisely because they depend on shift-by-shift detail, client location, and mode of travel, none of which a static pay rate captures.

**How software prevents it:** Allowances calculated from actual rostered travel and shift data, not applied as a flat rate or left to manual timesheet entry.

## 4. National Employment Standards entitlements missed alongside the award

The Agape matter is a useful reminder that SCHADS breaches rarely travel alone. The same investigation that flagged the casual worker's allowance shortfall also found the full-time employee had been underpaid annual leave entitlements under the [National Employment Standards (NES](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-vs-enterprise-agreement-disability-service)), a separate but equally enforceable set of minimum standards that sits alongside the award.

Providers often build strong award compliance while treating NES entitlements like leave accrual as a background payroll function, which is exactly where gaps open up.

**How software prevents it:** Leave accrual, entitlement balances, and award interpretation running in the same system, so NES and SCHADS obligations are checked together rather than in separate processes.

## 5. Broken shift and minimum engagement breaches

[Broken shifts](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches), where an employee's working day is split by an unpaid gap, and [minimum engagement periods for casuals](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-minimum-engagement) are two of the more technical corners of SCHADS, and among the easiest to get wrong manually. A single miscalculated broken shift allowance or a casual engaged under the two-hour minimum does not look dramatic on one payslip, but compounds fast across a large casual workforce running hundreds of short client visits a week.

**How software prevents it:** Shift structures validated against SCHADS minimum engagement and broken shift rules at the rostering stage, before the shift is even worked, not after payroll has already run.

## 6. Missing the annual wage review

SCHADS rates increase from the first full pay period on or after 1 July each year, following the Fair Work Commission's Annual Wage Review. Rates rose 3.5% from 1 July 2025, and a further 4.75% increase applies from 1 July 2026. Providers that update rates manually, or rely on someone remembering to check the Fair Work Ombudsman's pay guide, routinely run at least one full pay cycle at the old rate. Multiply that gap across a large workforce and it becomes a genuine underpayment, not just an administrative delay.

**How software prevents it:** Award rates that update centrally the moment the Fair Work Commission publishes new figures, so every future pay run reflects the correct rate without anyone needing to manually re-key it.

## 7. Record-keeping gaps that turn a small error into a big one

The Fair Work Ombudsman requires [payroll records, timesheets, and payslips](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-audit-guide-self-assess-fair-work) to be retained for at least seven years. Manual systems and spreadsheets rarely produce clean, audit-ready records over that timeframe, which matters enormously if a breach is ever found. It was self-reporting and a clear audit trail that allowed disability and community services provider Uniting Communities Incorporated to enter an Enforceable Undertaking with the Fair Work Ombudsman after identifying underpayments spanning November 2015 to December 2025 across its 65 South Australian sites. The organisation is returning more than $2.6 million, including superannuation and interest, to around 1,500 current and former employees.

That case is also a reminder of the scale that small, unnoticed errors can reach over a decade of manual or semi-manual payroll. Early self-reporting worked in Uniting Communities' favour, but the underlying issue, a decade of compounding award interpretation errors, is exactly what automated controls are designed to catch far earlier.

**How software prevents it:** Every shift, rate, and allowance calculation logged automatically, with a complete audit-ready history retained for the full statutory period, so a Fair Work investigation is a data export rather than a scramble.

## The pattern behind all seven

Every case above shares the same root cause: SCHADS is too complex, and changes too often, for manual processes or generic payroll software to track reliably. Sleepover rules alone have shifted three times in under twelve months. Rates change annually. Allowances depend on shift-level detail. None of that is a criticism of payroll or rostering teams. It is simply more variables than a spreadsheet was ever built to hold consistently correct.

Purpose-built SCHADS interpretation software closes that gap by encoding the award's rules directly into rostering and payroll, so compliance happens automatically at the point a shift is built, not months later when Fair Work comes asking questions.

# The Ultimate SCHADS Award Audit Guide: Self-Assess Before Fair Work Knocks

A practical SCHADS Audit guide for NDIS providers: sample audit queries, evidence pack structure, and the 7 highest-risk clauses Fair Work investigates first.

Disability and aged care is now a declared priority enforcement area for the Fair Work Ombudsman. In the 2024 to 2025 financial year, the regulator recovered more than $30 million in underpayments from the care sector, and since January 2025, intentional underpayment carries criminal penalties: the greater of $7.825 million or three times the underpayment amount for a company, and up to 10 years' imprisonment for individuals found guilty.

That is the backdrop every NDIS provider now operates in. The good news is that a genuine self-audit, done properly and before a regulator asks for one, is one of the few compliance activities that actually changes your outcome if something is wrong. This guide walks Directors and Compliance Leads through how Fair Work actually investigates, the seven SCHADS clauses that generate the most enforcement activity, sample queries to run against your own payroll data, and how to build an evidence pack that stands up to scrutiny.

## How Fair Work actually audits providers?

**Compliance notices.** Where the FWO has reasonable grounds to believe a contravention occurred, it can issue a compliance notice requiring the employer to calculate and rectify the underpayment within a set timeframe. This is typically how smaller, contained matters begin, as seen when the FWO issued a compliance notice to disability provider Agape in October 2024 over a $7,789.42 underpayment involving award allowances and NES leave entitlements.

**Enforceable Undertakings.** For larger or systemic issues, particularly where an employer self-reports, the FWO can accept an Enforceable Undertaking in place of court action. Disability and community services provider Uniting Communities Incorporated entered an Enforceable Undertaking after self-reporting underpayments spanning November 2015 to December 2025 across its 65 South Australian sites, returning more than $2.6 million to around 1,500 current and former employees. Self-reporting and a clear audit trail were central to that outcome.

**Litigation.** Where an employer disputes a compliance notice, or the FWO pursues a serious contravention through the courts, matters proceed to the Federal Circuit and Family Court or the Federal Court. This is also the pathway for genuine disputes about award interpretation, as seen in Jats Joint Pty Ltd v Fair Work Ombudsman [2025] FCA 743, where a disability provider successfully challenged the FWO's interpretation of sleepover shift penalties.

**The reverse onus of proof.** This is the detail most directors underestimate. Where an employer has failed to meet record-keeping or payslip obligations and cannot provide a reasonable excuse, the onus shifts: the employer must disprove the underpayment allegation, rather than the FWO proving it occurred. Poor records do not just make an audit harder. They can flip the legal burden onto you.

## The 7 highest-risk SCHADS clauses to audit first

### 1. Classification and pay point accuracy

SCHADS has [four streams and up to eight classification levels](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers), and the gap between them is material. A Level 2 worker in the Home Care and Disability stream sits on a different base rate to a Level 2 SACS stream worker, and some providers compound the risk by classifying support workers under the Home Care Award instead of SCHADS entirely.

**Audit query:** For a sample of 10 to 15 employees, does the assigned stream and level match their actual duties, independent of what payroll currently shows?

### 2. Sleepover and night shift loadings

This is the most contested area of the award, with the rules changing three times in under two years. The FWO originally treated work either side of a sleepover as one continuous shift, attracting a 15% loading. The Federal Court rejected that in Jats Joint, and the Full Federal Court dismissed the FWO's appeal in March 2026. The Fair Work Commission then varied the award itself: from the first full pay period on or after 1 June 2026, sleepovers again do not count as a break.

**Audit query:** For every [sleepover](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel) shift in the last 12 months, which rule set was applied, and does it match the legal position in force on that pay date?

### 3. Travel, transport, and fare allowances

These depend on [shift-by-shift detail](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately), client location, distance, and mode of travel, none of which a flat rate captures. This was central to the Agape matter, where a casual employee's underpayment included travel allowances alongside their minimum hourly rate.

**Audit query:** Do paid travel allowances match actual rostered travel distances, checked against roster data rather than payroll's own calculation?

### 4. NES entitlements alongside the award

SCHADS breaches rarely appear alone. In the Agape matter, the same investigation that found allowance shortfalls also found a full-time employee underpaid annual leave under the NES.

**Audit query:** For long-tenured employees, does accrued and paid leave match hours worked, including any leave periods that affect accrual?

### 5. Broken shifts and minimum engagement

[Broken shifts](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches) and [casual minimum engagement](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-minimum-engagement) periods are technically dense and easy to miscalculate manually. Errors rarely look dramatic on one payslip but compound fast across a large casual workforce.

**Audit query:** Were minimum engagement periods applied regardless of actual hours worked, and were broken shift allowances paid where the structure meets the award's definition?

### 6. Annual Wage Review timing

SCHADS rates increase from the first full pay period on or after 1 July each year. Rates rose 3.5% from 1 July 2025, with a further 4.75% increase from 1 July 2026. Providers relying on manual updates routinely miss the exact pay period boundary.

**Audit query:** For the pay period following each of the last three 1 July dates, were rates updated from the correct pay period, not the calendar date?

### 7. Record-keeping completeness

Employers must keep employee records for seven years and issue payslips within one working day of payment, legible, in English, and readily accessible on request.

**Audit query:** Can you produce, within 24 hours, seven years of payslips, timesheets, and classification history for any nominated employee? If the honest answer involves scattered systems or a former staff member's memory, that is your highest-priority fix, regardless of what the underlying pay data shows.

## Building your evidence pack

An evidence pack is the structured proof that your interpretation of SCHADS was reasonable, applied consistently, and can be reconstructed on request. At minimum, each employee file should produce:

- **Classification history,** including stream, level, and pay point at each point in employment, with reasoning for any changes.
- **Roster and timesheet records,** showing rostered versus actual hours and any sleepover, broken shift, or overtime components.
- **Allowance calculations,** showing how travel and other allowances were derived from actual shift data.
- **Leave accrual records,** reconciled against the NES, not just the award.
- **Payslips,** issued within one working day and containing everything required under the Fair Work Regulations.
- **A change log,** documenting when rate updates and interpretation changes, such as the June 2026 sleepover determination, were applied and from which pay period.

The organisations that come out of an FWO matter best, Uniting Communities among them, are the ones that can produce this kind of structured, dated evidence quickly. The ones that struggle are reconstructing history from memory and disconnected spreadsheets under time pressure.

## Running the self-audit

1. **Start with record-keeping, not pay accuracy.** Without clean records you cannot reliably audit anything else, and you are carrying the reverse onus risk regardless.
2. **Work through the seven clauses above in order,** using a meaningful sample rather than your whole workforce.
3. **Cross-reference against the NES, not just the award.** Leave and notice entitlements are just as enforceable.
4. **Quantify what you find.** A dollar figure and affected employee count turn a vague concern into an actionable plan.
5. **Decide on self-reporting early, with legal advice.** The Uniting Communities outcome shows early, transparent self-reporting materially changes how the FWO responds.
6. **Fix the system, not just the back pay.** A remediation payment addresses the past; only a change to [how rosters are built](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately) prevents the same clause failing again next quarter.

## Why manual audits struggle to keep up?

SCHADS changes more often than most modern awards. The sleepover rules alone applied three different legal positions within roughly eighteen months, each requiring different payroll treatment for the same shift type. A spreadsheet-based audit answers whether you were compliant on the day you checked. It cannot confirm that every pay period since your last audit applied the version of the rules actually in force at the time. Ongoing compliance needs [classification, allowance, and shift-penalty logic](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-breaches-fair-work-software-prevention) checked at the moment each shift is built and paid, not reconstructed months later.

## Turn this guide into an audit-ready system

Tesseractapps builds SCHADS award interpretation directly into rostering and payroll, so the checks in this guide run automatically on every shift rather than as a periodic manual exercise. For the full breakdown of classifications, allowances, and 2026 to 2027 transition dates, visit our SCHADS compliance hub and download the companion self-audit checklist to work through the seven clauses above against your own data.

Want to see how audit-ready your current rosters actually are? Book an audit-readiness demo and we will run a sample of your own data through the checks in this guide.

Tesseractapps runs these audit checks automatically on every shift. Visit [tesseractapps.com.au](https://tesseractapps.com.au) to book an audit-readiness demo.

# SCHADS vs Enterprise Agreement: Which Is Better for Your Disability Service?

Difference between SCHADS and  enterprise agreement in the Australian disability and community services sector with 2026 award changes in play.

If you run an NDIS or community services organisation, you have probably had this conversation at least once in the boardroom: should we stay on SCHADS, or is it time to negotiate our own enterprise agreement?

It is a fair question, and a timely one. The Fair Work Commission's June 2026 decision to overhaul SCHADS -a new classification structure, a wage reset, and the removal of the Equal Remuneration Order - has put award coverage back on the agenda for boards that had not touched their industrial instrument in years. With an interim pay rise for disability home care workers from October 2026, and a full restructure a year later, the question of which instrument to be on is now a budgeting question, not a theoretical one.

This article breaks down what SCHADS and an enterprise agreement actually offer disability providers, where each option helps or hurts, and the BOOT test traps that catch even experienced HR teams out.

## Quick refresher: what is the SCHADS Award?

The Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award sets [minimum pay and conditions](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers) for most disability support, home care, and community services workers in Australia. It is a modern award, meaning it is a safety net set centrally by the Fair Work Commission, not something your organisation negotiated.

SCHADS has long been criticised for being complex and inconsistent across its schedules, which is exactly what the Commission's 2026 gender-based undervaluation review set out to fix. The upshot: a new integrated classification structure is coming, home care and disability schedule employees get an interim increase from 1 October 2026, and the rest of the workforce transitions under the Final Classification Structure from 1 October 2027. Existing employees keep their current pay during translation, but the compliance workload of remapping every role is real.

## What is an enterprise agreement, and why do providers consider one?

An enterprise agreement, sometimes called an EBA, is a registered agreement negotiated directly between an employer and its employees, often with union involvement, covering wages and conditions in place of the award. Once employees vote to approve it, the employer lodges it with the Fair Work Commission for formal approval.

Providers move to an EBA to simplify a workforce that has outgrown award classifications, build in [rostering flexibility](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately) for 24/7 disability support work, trade off penalty rates for higher base pay, or gain more predictable and budgetable labour costs than an award that reshapes itself every few years. For some providers, a well-built NDIS enterprise agreement is the practical SCHADS alternative that finally matches how their rosters actually run.

## SCHADS vs enterprise agreement: the honest comparison

### Staying on SCHADS

**Pros:** No bargaining cost or timeline. Automatic compliance with award updates. Familiar to staff and easy to benchmark. No BOOT test exposure, since award minimums are already the floor you are paying to.

**Cons:** Limited flexibility on rostering and shift design. Minimal room to trade off conditions for operational needs. Right now, a period of genuine uncertainty as the new classification structure phases in over 2026 to 2027.

### Moving to an enterprise agreement

**Pros:** Tailored rostering and shift patterns that fit disability support delivery. Potential to simplify classifications for a large or mixed workforce. Greater cost predictability once locked in. An opportunity to modernise conditions that SCHADS was not designed for.

**Cons:** A genuine bargaining process with real time, cost, and industrial relations effort. A legal requirement to pass the BOOT test for every classification and roster pattern. Ongoing risk if your agreement falls behind future award increases. A real prospect of employee or union pushback during negotiation.

Neither option is universally better. A boutique provider with 20 support workers on fairly standard rosters may get little value from the cost and complexity of bargaining. A large provider running complex [24/7 rosters](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel) across multiple sites, with genuine flexibility needs, is far more likely to benefit from a tailored agreement - provided it is built and tested properly.

## The BOOT test: where enterprise agreements go wrong

The Better Off Overall Test is the single biggest hurdle to getting an enterprise agreement approved, and the single biggest source of failed applications in the disability and community services sector. The Fair Work Commission must be satisfied that every employee, in every classification and roster pattern the agreement covers, would be better off overall under the agreement than under the award.

The traps that catch providers out most often:

1. **Testing against today's SCHADS, not tomorrow's.** With the award mid-restructure, an agreement that clears the BOOT against current rates can fail against the new classification structure and wage rates rolling out from October 2026 and October 2027. Agreements need to be modelled against where the award is heading, not just where it sits today.
2. **Averaging across a group instead of testing each employee.** The BOOT is assessed employee by employee, or by representative work patterns, not as an average saving across the workforce. A roster pattern that is fine for day shift workers can fail for night shift or sleepover employees.
3. **Ignoring allowances and penalties in the trade-off.** Base rate increases that look generous on paper can still fail the BOOT once travel time, [sleepover provisions](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel), overtime, and allowances are properly accounted for. These are areas SCHADS treats in detail and that are easy to underweight in bargaining.
4. **Locking in terms without a wage review mechanism.** An agreement with no built-in increases can start compliant and quietly fall behind the award within a couple of wage reviews, creating a live BOOT problem later in the agreement's life, not just at approval. A wage review mechanism is essential, not optional.
5. **Underestimating sleepover and overnight shift complexity.** Following the Federal Court's ruling in the Jats Joint case, the Fair Work Commission's final determination confirmed that from 1 June 2026, a sleepover no longer counts as a break under SCHADS. Work performed either side of it is treated as one continuous shift. Any agreement covering overnight disability support needs sleepover and shift-loading provisions modelled against this current position, not a generic clause copied from another sector.

## Is now the right time to make the move?

Given the scale of the 2026 to 2027 SCHADS restructure, timing matters more than usual. Bargaining an agreement mid-overhaul without modelling the new classification structure is a good way to end up back at the Commission for a variation within 18 months. Waiting until October 2027 to even start the conversation, though, may leave cost and flexibility benefits on the table for a long transition period.

For most boards, the sensible sequence is: map your workforce against the incoming SCHADS classifications, model the [cost and compliance impact](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-to-manage-compliance-risk-ndis-providers), then decide whether an enterprise agreement justifies the bargaining effort -built to withstand the award as it will look in 2027, not just as it looks today.

## Which option is right for your organisation?

There is no one-size-fits-all answer, and providers who get burned usually picked a side before doing the modelling. The right call depends on your workforce size, roster complexity, growth plans, and appetite for an industrial relations process. What is consistent across the sector: getting the BOOT test wrong, or ignoring where SCHADS is heading, is an expensive mistake to unwind.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is an enterprise agreement always cheaper than SCHADS?

Not necessarily. An EBA can lower some costs, like penalty rates, while raising others, like base pay, and it must pass the BOOT test regardless. The real driver of value is usually rostering flexibility, not a straight wage discount.

### Can we move from SCHADS to an enterprise agreement at any time?

Yes, there is no fixed window, but bargaining takes time and must run in good faith. Given the current SCHADS restructure, most compliance advisors recommend modelling against the incoming award changes before locking in agreement terms.

### Does an enterprise agreement remove SCHADS coverage entirely?

Yes. Once an enterprise agreement is approved and in operation, it applies instead of the award for covered employees, though the award can still be relevant for interpreting entitlements not addressed in the agreement.

### What happens if our enterprise agreement fails the BOOT test later on?

The BOOT is assessed at approval, not continuously. But if [award increases](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates) later overtake your agreed rates, the agreement does not automatically become non-compliant; it becomes vulnerable to a variation application, a termination application, or pressure to renegotiate at the next bargaining round. This is why a built-in wage review or increase mechanism is essential, not optional.

For a full breakdown of SCHADS classifications, allowances, and 2026 to 2027 transition dates, see our SCHADS compliance hub. Weighing up SCHADS vs an enterprise agreement for your service? Talk to a compliance advisor before you model your next enterprise bargaining round.

Talk to a compliance advisor at [tesseractapps.com.au](https://tesseractapps.com.au) before you model your next enterprise bargaining round.

# Why NDIS Bulk Payment Claims Keep Getting Rejected (And How to Stop It Costing You Weekly)

PACE bulk upload rejections are silently eroding provider margins. The seven causes, how to prevent them, and what the fix costs weekly.

## A rejected NDIS claim isn't an error. It's a leak.

Under PACE, almost every payment request goes through the bulk upload process -even single claims. That means every rejected line item is not just an admin annoyance, it's revenue sitting in limbo. Multiply it by weekly claim runs, across dozens of participants, and you've built yourself a slow, quiet outflow that finance won't spot until end of quarter.

If your provider is submitting claims by uploading CSVs into the myplace portal and hoping for the best, this article is for you.

## The seven reasons NDIS bulk claims get rejected

Almost every rejection in the wild traces back to one of these:

1. Service booking mismatch. The line item is being claimed against a category, provider, or dates that don't line up with what's actually on the participant's plan under PACE. This is the number-one cause and the hardest to catch manually.
2. Support-item code errors. The wrong item number for the state, the wrong ratio for group supports, or a code that was quietly retired in the last price guide update.
3. Pricing above the cap. Someone put the raw internal rate into the bulk file instead of the NDIS-approved rate for that item, region, and time of day.
4. Overlapping service times. Two workers claiming for the same participant at the same minute -usually a rostering artefact from a copy-paste shift.
5. Plan expiry or plan review gap. The claim is dated inside a period where the participant's plan wasn't active, or where the new plan hadn't been re-endorsed.
6. Participant status change. The participant left your service, moved to a different plan management arrangement, or their consent has lapsed and nobody updated the record.
7. Bulk file structure errors. Wrong column order, missing mandatory fields, or a stale template pulled from a shared drive that nobody has updated since the last portal change.

## Why 'we'll clean it up on Friday' is a losing strategy

Under PACE, a rejected claim can't just be fixed inline. The rejected line has to be removed, corrected, and re-submitted as a new payment request. If your team is doing that in a spreadsheet, you're carrying three costs:

- The re-work labour -often 15 to 40 minutes per rejection, across support workers, coordinators, and finance.
- The cashflow gap -the claim sits unpaid until it's re-submitted and cleared. On a mid-size provider that can be tens of thousands rolling forward month on month.
- The audit exposure -rejections that never get re-submitted look like unbilled service delivery, which is a red flag the moment an internal audit or Commission review starts pulling records.

## How to stop claim rejections before they happen

### 1. Validate at the point of rostering, not the point of upload

If your platform lets a support worker be rostered for a shift the participant's plan can't fund, the rejection is already baked in. NDIS-native operational platforms check service bookings, support-item codes, and pricing at the moment a shift is scheduled -hours or days before the claim is generated.

### 2. Generate the bulk file from service delivery data, not from a spreadsheet

Every re-keyed value between the roster, the timesheet, and the bulk upload is a rejection waiting to happen. The claim file should be a read-only export of what actually happened in service delivery, generated by the same system that scheduled and delivered the shift.

### 3. Track rejections with a reason code, an owner, and an SLA

A rejection dashboard with reason codes and named owners turns a mystery into a manageable process. Fifteen rejections a week with clear owners and a two-day fix SLA is a normal operation. Fifteen rejections a week piling up in a shared inbox is a crisis in slow motion.

### 4. Reconcile weekly, not monthly

The gap between service delivery and payment should be measured in days, not weeks. Weekly reconciliation catches PACE issues while the shift is still fresh in the worker's memory and the participant's record is still current.

## What a fixed workflow looks like

On a modern NDIS operational platform, the ideal claim run looks like this: a shift is rostered against the participant's service booking; the platform validates that the booking, item code, and rate all agree; the shift is delivered and the worker clocks off; the claim line is generated automatically; the bulk file is submitted; the response file is reconciled inside the platform, with rejections routed to an owner and a re-submission workflow.

If that's not what your Fridays look like, your platform is costing you more than its licence fee.

# Best NDIS Software in 2026

Compare NDIS software the way a CFO would - architecture, governance and true year-two cost, not just a feature grid.

## Every 'best NDIS software' list looks the same. Yours probably shouldn't.

Search 'best NDIS software' and you'll get thirty listicles that grade platforms on the same tired criteria -rostering, invoicing, mobile app, 'user-friendly interface.' That's a checklist a 2019 aged-care buyer would recognise. It is not the criteria that will keep your registration in 2026.

If you're evaluating NDIS software this year, the decision is no longer about features. Every serious platform has features. The decision is about architecture, governance, and whether the tool you sign onto can survive the next audit, the next PACE change, and the next SCHADS interpretation without a project manager, a consultant, and a six-figure invoice.

Here is the buyer's guide the top of Google won't give you.

## Ignore the feature grid. Ask these four questions instead.

### 1. Is it NDIS-native or NDIS-adapted?

A lot of software marketed to NDIS providers was originally built for allied health clinics, aged care rosters, or generic small-business ops. It was retrofitted. You can tell within ten minutes of a demo -the price guide lives in a spreadsheet the vendor exports, SCHADS is 'on the roadmap', and SIRS reporting means an email template.

NDIS-native platforms are architected around the Quality and Safeguards Commission, the price guide, PACE claiming, and SCHADS obligations from day one. They don't 'support' the NDIS. They assume it.

### 2. Is it one platform, or a bundle wearing a costume?

Some of the biggest names in the category are actually three or four acquisitions bolted together. The demo looks unified. The invoice, the implementation timeline, and the data-reconciliation headaches say otherwise.

Ask the vendor a specific question: 'When a shift is rostered, does the same record become the timesheet, the payroll entry, the participant service note, and the NDIS bulk-upload line item -or does data move between systems?' If the answer includes the words 'integration' or 'sync', it's a bundle.

### 3. Where does your participant data physically live?

Sensitive participant data has to meet Australian data-sovereignty expectations. Some platforms host in Australia. Some claim to. Some are genuinely built on enterprise-grade Australian infrastructure like Salesforce Hyperforce, which meets the standard most auditors are quietly starting to expect.

Ask for the region, the hosting provider, the certifications (SOC 2 Type II is the floor, not the ceiling), and the sub-processor list. If the vendor hesitates on any of these, keep walking.

### 4. What does year two actually cost?

Year one pricing is bait. Year two is where a per-module, per-user, per-participant, per-integration platform reveals what it really costs. Ask for a written year-two quote at 1.5x your current headcount. The vendors who don't blink are the ones worth shortlisting.

## What 'best' looks like in 2026

The providers we see thriving right now share four operational traits, and their software has to enable each one:

- SCHADS Award interpretation is enforced at the roster, not caught at payroll. Sleepovers, active nights, broken shifts, and minimum engagements are classified when the shift is created -not corrected on Friday.
- PACE bulk uploads reconcile automatically. Rejected line items surface with a reason code, an owner, and a re-submission workflow -not as a mystery balance the bookkeeper discovers weeks later.
- Incidents move on rails. From frontline capture to SIRS notification to root-cause and learnings, one record, one timeline, one auditable chain.
- Compliance is continuous. Credential expiries, restrictive-practice registers, participant reviews, and worker screening statuses are dashboarded -not chased quarterly by a QA officer with a to-do list.

## The uncomfortable truth about 'all-in-one'

Every vendor calls themselves all-in-one. Very few actually are. The test is simple: can one platform, from one login, run intake, rostering, SCHADS-aware payroll prep, participant records, service delivery, NDIS claiming, incident management, and board-level reporting -without any 'integration partner'?

If the answer is yes, you have a genuine operational platform. If the answer is 'yes, with our integration to X', you have a stack, and you'll pay for it in reconciliation labour every fortnight for as long as you own it.

## Shortlist the shortlist

Once you've asked the four questions and stress-tested the 'all-in-one' claim, most 'best NDIS software' lists will collapse down to a handful of serious candidates. From there, the final filter is cultural: does the vendor treat NDIS providers as a specialist market, or as one vertical among many?

Providers who pick a specialist tend to still be on that platform five years later. Providers who pick a generalist tend to be running an RFP again in eighteen months. Choose accordingly.

# Calculating Overtime, Public Holiday and Weekend Penalties Under SCHADS

Step-by-step worked examples of SCHADS overtime, weekend and public holiday pay, including QLD, NSW, VIC, WA holiday variations.

Penalty rates are where the SCHADS Award gets expensive fast. What payroll owes on any given shift depends on the day, the time, the stream and whether hours pushed past ordinary limits. Get one variable wrong and the error repeats on every similar shift until someone does the audit.

This guide sets out every penalty rate, overtime rate and public holiday rate under the SCHADS Award with step-by-step worked examples and a state-by-state public holiday table. All rates reflect the 4.75% increase effective from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026.

## Weekend penalty rates under SCHADS

Weekend rates under the award are expressed as multiples of the ordinary base rate. They apply to all ordinary hours worked on Saturday and Sunday and differ between permanent and casual employees because the 25% casual loading stacks on top of the penalty for weekends and public holidays.

| Day | Permanent (FT/PT) | Casual |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Saturday | 150% | 175% |
| Sunday | 200% | 225% |
| Public holiday | 250% | 275% |


For a permanent Level 2 SACS employee at an indicative 2026 base of $36.22/hr:

- Saturday rate: $54.33/hr
- Sunday rate: $72.44/hr
- Public holiday rate: $90.55/hr

For a casual at the same level (indicative base $45.28/hr including loading):

- Saturday: $63.39/hr (175% of $36.22)
- Sunday: $81.50/hr (225% of $36.22)
- Public holiday: $99.61/hr (275% of $36.22)

The casual calculation applies the loading to the base rate, then multiplies by the penalty percentage. It does not simply add 25% to the permanent penalty rate.

## Shift loadings: afternoons and nights

Shift loadings apply to the whole shift, not just the hours that fall outside ordinary time. If a shift finishes after 8pm on a Monday to Friday, the entire shift attracts the afternoon loading. If it finishes after midnight or starts before 6am Monday to Friday, it attracts the night loading.

| Shift type | Loading |
| --- | --- |
| Afternoon (finishes after 8pm Mon-Fri) | 112.5% of base rate |
| Night (finishes after midnight or starts before 6am Mon-Fri) | 115% of base rate |


Shift loadings and weekend penalties do not stack. Only the higher rate applies. A shift that finishes after 8pm on a Friday attracts the afternoon loading or the Friday ordinary rate, whichever is higher. The same shift on a Saturday attracts the Saturday penalty rate, not the Saturday rate plus an afternoon loading.

## Overtime rates by stream

SCHADS overtime rates are where the stream distinction matters most. The point at which the higher rate kicks in differs between streams.

**SACS and Crisis Accommodation employees (Schedules B and C):**

- Monday to Saturday overtime: 150% for the first three hours, 200% after that
- Sunday overtime: 200% for all hours
- Public holiday overtime: 250% for all hours

**Home Care, Disability Services and Family Day Care employees (Schedules D, E and F):**

- Monday to Saturday overtime: 150% for the first two hours, 200% after that
- Sunday overtime: 200% for all hours
- Public holiday overtime: 250% for all hours

The difference between a two-hour and three-hour first band matters on long shifts. A SACS worker doing four hours of overtime on a Saturday has 150% applying for the first three hours and 200% for the fourth. A Home Care employee doing the same four hours tips into 200% after just two.

Overtime rates replace weekend and penalty rates. They do not stack on top of them. A Sunday overtime hour is paid at 200%, not at 200% Sunday penalty plus overtime uplift. The higher of the two applicable rates applies.

Overtime is triggered when an employee works beyond their rostered hours, exceeds 38 hours in a week (averaged), or works outside the ordinary span of hours (broadly 6am to 8pm Monday to Sunday for most SCHADS roles). Casuals attract overtime after more than 10 hours in a day or 38 hours in a week, always applying the first band rate.

## A worked example: permanent SACS Level 2 working a long Saturday

A permanent Level 2 SACS employee at $36.22/hr base is rostered 8am to 5pm on a Saturday, but stays until 7pm covering a staff shortage.

- 8am to 5pm (9 hours ordinary Saturday work): 150% x $36.22 = $54.33/hr x 9 = $489.00
- 5pm to 7pm (2 hours Saturday overtime, within the 3-hour first band): 150% x $36.22 = $54.33/hr x 2 = $108.66

Total before super: $597.66 for the 11-hour Saturday. If the same worker had stayed until 8:30pm, the final 1.5 hours beyond the 3-hour overtime threshold would move to 200% ($72.44/hr).

## A worked example: casual Home Care Level 2 on a public holiday

A casual Home Care Disability Level 2 employee has an indicative 2026 base of approximately $28.86/hr. On a public holiday they earn 275% of the base rate: $28.86 x 2.75 = $79.37/hr. A three-hour visit pays approximately $238.10 before super and allowances, and with the two-hour minimum engagement, a 90-minute visit still costs $158.74. That is the figure the NDIS public holiday price limit has to cover.

## State-by-state public holiday variations: why the date matters

The SCHADS Award sets a flat 250% (permanent) or 275% (casual) rate for any work performed on a public holiday. What varies by state is which days qualify as public holidays in the first place.

NDIS providers operating across multiple states may have workers entitled to public holiday pay on different dates for the same service type. A worker in Queensland working on Queensland Labour Day earns 250% for that day. A worker in Victoria doing the same work on the same date earns their ordinary rate because Victoria's Labour Day falls in March, not May.

The table below covers the key state-specific public holidays most likely to affect disability and community services rosters in 2026.

| State | State-specific public holidays 2026 | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| QLD | Labour Day: Mon 4 May; Royal Queensland Show (Ekka): Wed 12 Aug; Christmas Eve part-day: 25 Dec from 6pm | Ekka applies to Brisbane area only; Christmas Eve is a part-day public holiday from 6pm |
| VIC | Labour Day: Mon 9 March; AFL Grand Final Friday: date TBC; Melbourne Cup Day: Tue 3 Nov | AFL Grand Final Friday date subject to AFL schedule; Melbourne Cup Day applies statewide unless local arrangement |
| NSW | King's Birthday: Mon 8 June; Labour Day: Mon 5 Oct | ANZAC Day substitute: Mon 27 April (Sat 25 April is ANZAC Day, NSW observes substitute) |
| WA | Labour Day: Mon 2 March; WA Day: Mon 1 June; King's Birthday: Mon 28 Sept | Regional areas may observe King's Birthday on a different date |
| SA | Adelaide Cup: Mon 9 March; King's Birthday: Mon 8 June; Labour Day: Mon 5 Oct; Christmas Eve part-day: 25 Dec from 7pm; New Year's Eve part-day: 31 Dec from 7pm | Part-day holidays from 7pm only |
| ACT | Canberra Day: Mon 9 March; Reconciliation Day: Mon 25 May; King's Birthday: Mon 8 June; Labour Day: Mon 5 Oct | 15 public holidays in 2026, highest in Australia |


National public holidays in 2026 apply across all states: New Year's Day, Australia Day, Good Friday, Easter Monday, ANZAC Day, Christmas Day and Boxing Day substitute (Mon 28 Dec in most states). One scheduling note: ANZAC Day falls on Saturday 25 April. Only ACT, NSW and WA observe a substitute Monday. In Victoria, Queensland, South Australia and Tasmania the public holiday pay applies on the Saturday itself, and Monday 27 April is an ordinary weekday.

## How overtime interacts with public holidays?

Work on a public holiday that runs into overtime is paid at 250% for all hours. The public holiday rate replaces other penalty and overtime rates for those hours. A worker recalled after finishing their rostered hours on a public holiday is paid at 250% for each hour worked, subject to the applicable minimum engagement period.

## Common payroll errors with penalties and overtime

**Applying the wrong overtime band for the stream.** SACS employees get three hours at 150% before moving to 200%. Home Care and Disability Services employees move after two. Applying the two-hour rule uniformly across all streams understates the 150% band for every SACS and crisis worker.

**Stacking loadings that should not stack.** Afternoon loading and Saturday penalty do not apply simultaneously. Only the Saturday penalty applies on a Saturday evening. An evening loading on top of that is an overpayment that complicates reconciliation when rates change.

**Missing state-specific public holidays for multi-state providers.** A roster built around national public holidays only misses state-specific dates entirely, creating public holiday underpayments for every affected worker on those dates.

**Using the casual rate as the base for penalty calculations.** The penalty percentage applies to the base rate, not the casual-loaded rate. Saturday casual at 175% means $36.22 x 1.75 = $63.39, not $45.28 x 1.50.

## Getting penalty calculations right across a full roster

Penalty rates under SCHADS interact with stream, employment type, time of day, day of week and whether hours exceed ordinary limits. A payroll officer manually calculating these across a large roster is one configuration error away from a systematic underpayment.

TesseractApps applies SCHADS penalty rates, overtime thresholds and public holiday rates inside the payroll module automatically, with state-specific public holiday calendars built in so a Queensland Christmas Eve part-day or Victorian Melbourne Cup Day applies without a manual flag. **Book a demo** to see how it handles your workforce and roster mix.

## SCHADS overtime and penalty rates FAQ

#### **What is the Saturday penalty rate under SCHADS?** 

150% of the base rate for permanent full-time and part-time employees, 175% for casuals. At an indicative 2026 Level 2 SACS base of $36.22/hr, the Saturday permanent rate is approximately $54.33/hr and the casual rate approximately $63.39/hr.

#### **What is the Sunday rate under SCHADS?**

200% for permanent employees, 225% for casuals. At Level 2 SACS these work out to approximately $72.44/hr permanent and $81.50/hr casual.

#### **What is the public holiday rate under SCHADS?** 

250% for permanent employees, 275% for casuals. At Level 2 SACS these work out to approximately $90.55/hr permanent and $99.61/hr casual.

#### **Does overtime stack on top of weekend penalties under SCHADS?** 

No. Overtime rates replace weekend and penalty rates. A Sunday overtime hour is 200%, not 200% plus an overtime uplift.

#### **How does SCHADS overtime differ by stream?** 

SACS and Crisis Accommodation employees: 150% for the first three overtime hours, 200% after. Home Care, Disability Services and Family Day Care: 150% for the first two overtime hours, 200% after. Sunday and public holiday overtime is 200% and 250% respectively for all streams.

#### **Do state public holidays affect SCHADS penalty rates?** 

Yes. The 250% (permanent) or 275% (casual) public holiday rate applies on any day that is a public holiday in the relevant state. State-specific holidays such as QLD Labour Day, VIC Melbourne Cup Day and WA Day affect which days attract public holiday rates and vary by state.

_This guide is general information only and does not constitute legal or workplace relations advice. Confirm current rates and your obligations with the [Fair Work Ombudsman](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/) on 13 13 94 and the official MA000100 pay guide._

# Minimum Engagement Periods Under SCHADS: The 2-Hour Rule and Common Pitfalls

What counts toward minimum engagement under SCHADS, how breaks affect it, and the pitfalls Fair Work auditors flag most often.

Of all the ways NDIS providers end up with an underpayment liability, missing minimum engagement periods is one of the most avoidable. The rule is straightforward, the dollar value on any single shift is small, and that combination is exactly why it accumulates quietly for years before anyone notices. The Fair Work Ombudsman recovered more than $30 million in underpayments from the care sector in 2024-25. Minimum engagement was cited as one of the most frequent causes alongside misclassification and broken shift allowances. World Vision Australia repaid over $6 million in June 2024. Open Minds Australia paid $4.2 million in May 2024. These were not small operators with manual payroll and no HR function. They were established organisations.

Since January 2025, intentional underpayment is a criminal offence. A payroll configuration someone knowingly chose, even years ago, is potentially in scope. This guide covers exactly how the SCHADS minimum engagement rules work under clause 10.5, which employees they apply to, how breaks affect them, and where Fair Work auditors find the gaps.

## What the award actually says?

Clause 10.5 of the SCHADS Award sets minimum payment obligations for part-time and casual employees. It is not a general rule about shift length for everyone under the award. It applies specifically to two employment types: part-time and casual. Full-time employees are governed by their contracted hours and the ordinary hours provisions, not clause 10.5.

Within those two employment types, the minimum varies by stream and role:

**Three hours per shift** applies to social and community services employees, except when they are performing disability services work.

**Two hours per shift** applies to all other employees under the award: home care employees, crisis accommodation employees, family day care employees, and SACS employees who are performing disability services work.

That distinction between SACS-non-disability and SACS-disability is one of the most commonly misread rules in the award. A support coordinator doing non-disability case management is on a three-hour minimum. A SACS employee delivering direct disability support is on two hours. Applying the wrong minimum to the wrong role is an error that repeats every pay cycle.

## What "minimum engagement" actually means in practice?

The minimum engagement period is the minimum amount of time a part-time or casual employee must be paid for each shift or work period, regardless of how long they actually worked.

A casual support worker rostered for a one-hour community access visit must be paid for two hours at the applicable rate, including the casual loading and any penalty rates for the day or time. A part-time SACS employee rostered for a two-hour wellness check must be paid for three hours if they are doing non-disability work. The worker leaving after 45 minutes, or the visit running short because the participant cancelled partway through, does not reduce the minimum payment obligation.

This is the part that surprises most rostering coordinators. The minimum is not a floor on the shift as scheduled. It is a floor on the payment, regardless of what actually happens on the day.

## How minimum engagement interacts with broken shifts?

Each work period within a broken shift must independently meet the minimum engagement requirement. A broken shift is not assessed as a whole against the daily minimum. It is assessed period by period.

A home care worker rostered for a 90-minute morning visit and a 90-minute afternoon visit with an unpaid break in between has two work periods that each fall below the two-hour minimum. Both must be paid as two hours. The shift costs the employer four hours of pay, plus the broken shift allowance, for three hours of actual work. A roster built around 90-minute visits across a split day is systematically underpaying unless it is calculating each period against the minimum.

This is one of the most common patterns CrossVault and other SCHADS audit tools flag in timesheet reviews: visits of 60 to 90 minutes paired into broken shifts, with payroll calculating actual time rather than minimum time for each period.

## Client cancellations and the minimum engagement obligation

Under clause 25.5, if a client cancels with less than seven days notice, the employer can redirect the worker to other duties. If redirection is not possible, the employer may cancel the shift but must pay the employee the amount they would have received, or provide make-up time within six weeks. For same-day cancellations, the minimum engagement obligation applies the moment the worker presents for duty. A worker who arrives at a participant's home to find the service cancelled must still be paid for the minimum period. The obligation does not disappear because the participant was unavailable.

## The Woolworths ruling and why each pay period matters

The Federal Court's September 2025 decision in _Fair Work Ombudsman v Woolworths Group Limited_ [2025] FCA 1092 confirmed that overpayments in one pay period cannot offset underpayments in another, and each entitlement must be satisfied separately. A roster that overpays some workers on some shifts gives no credit against minimum engagement shortfalls elsewhere. The shortfalls accumulate across the six-year period the Fair Work Ombudsman can examine.

## The most common minimum engagement errors

**Calculating actual time instead of minimum time.** The most basic error, and the most widespread. Payroll systems that record actual clock-in and clock-out times and pay on the minute have no mechanism to apply the two or three-hour floor unless that rule has been explicitly configured. A system paying 73 minutes for a 73-minute visit is not compliant. Someone has to have set up the minimum engagement top-up, or it does not apply.

**Applying the wrong minimum to the role.** Three hours for non-disability SACS, two hours for everyone else. The error usually runs in one direction: applying two hours to SACS employees doing non-disability coordination work where three hours should apply. Less commonly, three hours gets applied to disability support workers where two is correct. Both are wrong.

**Excluding casuals from the minimum.** Some providers operate on the assumption that casuals, because they are paid per shift with a loading, are not covered by minimum engagement. They are. The casual loading compensates for the absence of paid leave. It does not substitute for the minimum engagement obligation. A casual on a 45-minute shift must still be paid for two hours at their full casual rate including penalty rates for the time of day.

**Missing the per-period rule in broken shifts.** As above: each work period in a broken shift carries its own minimum. A shift with two periods of 75 minutes each is two separate underpayments, not one shift that totals 150 minutes.

**Treating cancellation as cancellation of the obligation.** If a worker presents for duty and the service is cancelled, the minimum engagement clock has already started.

## What Fair Work auditors actually look for?

The Fair Work Ombudsman's compliance approach has shifted toward data-led auditing. Pattern detection flags providers whose payroll shows a concentration of shifts paid at exactly the visit duration: 60 minutes, 90 minutes, 120 minutes. A roster of 90-minute visits with 90-minute payments across a casual workforce surfaces quickly. A single complaint can open a full audit covering all employees, with records examinable back seven years. Penalties reach $93,900 per contravention for a small business employer and $939,000 for serious contraventions. With minimum engagement applying to every work period of every affected employee, systemic errors produce a large number of contraventions fast.

## Getting the configuration right

The fix requires the payroll system to know which rule applies to which employee: stream, role type (SACS disability versus SACS non-disability), and employment type all need to be correctly configured before the minimum engagement rule can fire automatically. TesseractApps applies minimum engagement rules inside the rostering module as shifts are built, flagging periods below the applicable minimum before the roster goes out. A 75-minute visit for a casual home care worker automatically calculates as two hours at the correct rate without a separate manual step. Talk to the compliance team about configuration for your workforce mix.

## Minimum engagement under SCHADS FAQ

**What is the minimum engagement period under SCHADS?** 

Two hours per shift or work period for most employees, including home care workers, disability support workers, crisis accommodation staff and SACS employees doing disability services work. Three hours per shift for SACS employees performing non-disability social and community services work.

**Does the minimum engagement apply to casual employees?** 

Yes. The two-hour and three-hour minimums apply to both part-time and casual employees under clause 10.5 of the SCHADS Award. The casual loading does not substitute for the minimum engagement obligation.

**Does the minimum engagement apply per broken shift or per work period?** Per work period. Each separate period of work within a broken shift must independently meet the two-hour or three-hour minimum.

**What happens if a client cancels and the worker has already arrived?** 

The minimum engagement obligation applies from the moment the worker presents for duty. A same-day cancellation does not remove the obligation to pay the minimum engagement period. The employer must pay the applicable minimum or provide make-up time within six weeks, depending on the circumstances.

**Can overpayments on other shifts offset minimum engagement shortfalls?** No. Following the Federal Court's 2025 decision in FWO v Woolworths, overpayments in one pay period cannot offset underpayments in another, and each entitlement must be satisfied separately.

**How far back can Fair Work audit minimum engagement underpayments?** Seven years under the Fair Work Act, though the standard limitation period for court proceedings is six years. A single complaint can trigger an audit covering all employees, not just the complainant.

_This guide is general information only and does not constitute legal or workplace relations advice. Confirm your specific obligations with the [Fair Work Ombudsman](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/) on 13 13 94 or a qualified workplace relations adviser._
