# Sleepover Allowance, Active Hours and Travel Time: SCHADS Made Simple 

Sleepovers, active hours and client travel under SCHADS — how to calculate, code and pay correctly in Australian SIL and in-home services. 

Three provisions sit at the heart of almost every SIL and in-home support roster under the [SCHADS Award](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-2026-the-complete-guide-for-ndis-and-disability-providers), and three provisions are where the payroll errors concentrate. Sleepovers, active overnight hours and travel time between clients are each governed by specific clauses in the award, each has its own rate, and each interacts with the others in ways that a flat hourly rate calculation will never capture. If your organisation delivers overnight supports, Supported Independent Living or multiple home visits in a single day, this is the part of the award that will determine whether your payroll is compliant.

This guide covers all three: what the award says, how the 2026 rates work, and what the June sleepover variation means for your SIL payroll now.

## Sleepovers under SCHADS: what the award actually says? 

A sleepover under clause 25.7 of the SCHADS Award is a specific type of overnight arrangement where an employee is required by the employer to remain at the workplace or participant's home overnight, is permitted to sleep, and is available to assist if needed. It is not a shift. It is not a rest break. And it is not the same as an active overnight shift where the worker is awake and working throughout.

Getting that distinction right matters because the two are paid completely differently.

A sleepover attracts a flat allowance of 4.9% of the standard rate per continuous 8-hour sleepover period. The standard rate is the minimum pay for a SCHADS Social and Community Services employee at Level 3 Pay Point 3. From 1 July 2026, that works out to approximately $62.87 per sleepover night, after the 4.75% annual wage review increase. That allowance covers the entire sleepover period. The worker is not paid an hourly rate for the hours they are asleep.

There are two other requirements that attach to every legitimate sleepover. First, at least one of the periods of work immediately before or immediately after the sleepover must be rostered or paid as a minimum of four hours. A sleepover that floats in isolation with a 30-minute handover on each side does not meet this requirement. Second, if the employee is woken during the sleepover to perform work, that call-to-duty is paid at overtime rates with a minimum payment of one hour per call-out, regardless of how brief the actual intervention was.

## What changed on 1 June 2026?

FWC decision [2025] FWCFB 292, handed down in December 2025, took effect from the first full pay period on or after 1 June 2026. Two things changed that every SIL manager needs to understand.

The work immediately before and immediately after a sleepover is now treated as a single continuous shift for overtime purposes. Under the previous interpretation, a six-hour evening block and a four-hour morning block could be read as two separate shifts. From 1 June 2026 they are one shift with ten combined hours of active work, assessed as a single engagement against overtime thresholds.

A sleepover also no longer counts as a rest break between the work periods that surround it. You cannot treat the sleepover as satisfying the rest requirement between the evening and morning blocks. The rest entitlement sits separately and still needs to be met.

One thing that did not change: the 15% night shift loading does not apply to work simply because it adjoins a sleepover. Confirmed by the Full Federal Court in [2026] FCAFC 25. Work on each side of the sleepover is assessed on its own time-of-day profile.

## Active overnight hours: a completely different calculation 

An active overnight shift is one where the employee is awake and working throughout. There is no sleepover allowance. There is no passive period. The worker performs care, supervision or other duties continuously, and every hour is paid at the applicable time-of-day and day-of-week penalty rate.

The cost difference between the two is significant. A sleepover with no call-to-duty costs the provider $62.87 in allowance plus adjacent shift hours. An active overnight shift from 10pm to 6am for a Level 2 SACS worker attracts night penalty rates on every hour, which is why some providers try to roster what is functionally an active night as a sleepover. The Fair Work Ombudsman is alert to this. The test is whether the employee is genuinely permitted to sleep and only required to provide assistance if needed. A worker who must maintain awareness and respond frequently throughout the night is not on a sleepover, regardless of what the roster says.

## Travel time between clients: what is paid and what is not?

Travel time under the SCHADS Award is governed by clauses 20.2 and 20.3. Travel between clients during a shift is paid at the worker's ordinary rate and counts toward total hours worked, minimum engagement and overtime thresholds. Travel from the worker's home to the first client, and from the last client home, is not paid.

When a worker uses their own vehicle between clients or to transport a participant, a vehicle allowance applies. From 1 July 2026, that rate is $1.01 per kilometre under clause 20.3, up from $0.99/km in 2025-26. It covers fuel, depreciation and running costs. Reasonable parking and tolls during the shift can be reimbursed separately. Workers should record start and finish addresses and total kilometres for the day. The allowance applies equally when driving a participant to an appointment, not just when travelling empty between locations.

## How the three provisions interact in a SIL roster?

Take a support worker in a SIL house who works the following pattern on a Wednesday:

- 3pm to 9pm: active support (six hours)
- 9pm to 7am: sleepover (ten hours, permitted to sleep)
- 7am to 11am: morning support (four hours)

From 1 June 2026, the 3pm to 9pm shift and the 7am to 11am shift are treated as a single continuous shift of ten active hours. Overtime thresholds are assessed on the combined ten hours, not on each block separately. The sleepover period from 9pm to 7am is paid at the flat $62.87 allowance. If the worker is woken at 2am to assist a participant, that intervention is paid at overtime rates with a one-hour minimum.

By agreement, a shift including a sleepover can have up to 12 hours of active work, with a cap of eight ordinary hours on each side. Six hours before and four hours after sits within that cap, so no overtime applies on the active hours alone, though stream-specific thresholds still need checking. If the same worker travelled from a previous client to the SIL house at 2:45pm, those travel minutes are paid work time and the kilometres attract the $1.01/km vehicle allowance. The drive from their home to the previous client is not paid.

## Common mistakes in SIL and overnight payroll 

Treating the sleepover as a rest break between shifts is now a breach since 1 June 2026. Providers relying on the sleepover to satisfy the rest requirement between evening and morning blocks need to review their SIL rosters.

Not meeting the four-hour minimum on either side is another common gap. The award requires at least one adjacent work period of four hours. A two-hour handover on both sides does not satisfy this.

Calculating the call-to-duty minimum incorrectly is a recurring error. A 15-minute bed repositioning at 3am is still paid as one hour at overtime rates. The five-minute actual duration is irrelevant.

On travel, the most common mistake is not capturing it. Workers who do not record travel time and kilometres between clients means the entitlement never reaches payroll, producing an underpayment on every shift involving client-to-client travel.

## How purpose-built SIL rostering helps? 

Managing sleepovers, active overnight hours, travel time and the post-June 2026 continuity rules across a full SIL roster requires software that understands the specific clauses, not just the base rate. The interaction between pre-sleepover hours, post-sleepover hours and the continuity rule alone is difficult to track on a spreadsheet, particularly across a house running multiple workers on rotating overnight patterns.

TesseractApps applies SCHADS sleepover rules, active hour rates, travel pay and vehicle allowance triggers inside the SIL rostering module, updated to reflect the 1 June 2026 variation. A call-to-duty during a sleepover calculates at the correct overtime rate automatically, and travel kilometres on the timesheet generate the $1.01/km allowance line without a separate calculation. Download the free SCHADS Checklist to work through every sleepover, active night and travel obligation before your next SIL pay run.

## Sleepover, active hours and travel FAQ 

### What is the SCHADS sleepover allowance in 2026? 

Approximately $62.87 per sleepover night from 1 July 2026, reflecting the 4.75% annual wage review increase. It is 4.9% of the standard rate (SACS Level 3 Pay Point 3) under clause 25.7(d). Confirm the exact figure against the Fair Work Ombudsman's MA000100 pay guide.

### What changed about SCHADS sleepovers on 1 June 2026? 

From the first full pay period on or after 1 June 2026, following FWC decision [2025] FWCFB 292, work before and after a sleepover is treated as a single continuous shift for overtime purposes. A sleepover also no longer counts as a rest break between shifts under clause 25.4.

### What is the minimum payment if a worker is woken during a sleepover? 

One hour at overtime rates per call-out, regardless of how brief the actual work was. If the worker is woken twice, each call-out attracts its own one-hour minimum.

### Is travel time between clients paid under SCHADS? 

Yes. Travel time between clients during a shift is paid at the worker's ordinary rate. Travel from home to the first client and from the last client home is not paid.

### What is the SCHADS vehicle allowance in 2026? 

$1.01 per kilometre from 1 July 2026 under clause 20.3, up from $0.99/km in 2025-26. It applies when a worker uses their own vehicle between clients or to transport a participant.

### What is the difference between a sleepover and an active overnight shift? 

A sleepover is where the employee is permitted to sleep and only required to assist if needed, paid at the flat $62.87 allowance per night. An active overnight shift is where the employee is awake and working throughout, paid at applicable hourly and penalty rates for every hour worked.

# Broken Shifts Under SCHADS: How to Roster Without Breaching the Award?

How the broken-shift clause works under SCHADS, when allowances apply, and rostering patterns AU providers use to stay compliant?

Broken shifts are one of those SCHADS provisions that everyone in rostering knows about and almost no-one fully understands. The allowance is small enough that providers sometimes ignore it, and the eligibility rules are specific enough that applying it to the wrong employees creates a different kind of problem. Between under-applying it, over-applying it, and rostering past the 12-hour span without noticing, broken shifts generate more avoidable compliance exposure than almost anything else in the award.

This guide covers who the broken shift rules apply to, how the allowance works, what the [rostering ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/capabilities/rostering-scheduling)constraints actually are, and how to build compliant split-day patterns around the way NDIS supports are delivered.

## What is a broken shift under SCHADS? 

Under clause 25.6 of the SCHADS Award, a broken shift is a shift worked in two or more separate periods of work within a single day, with an unpaid break in between that is not a meal break. The distinction matters. A 30-minute unpaid lunch in the middle of a continuous shift is not a broken shift. A three-hour unpaid gap between a morning and an afternoon block is.

This is the pattern that shows up constantly in NDIS community access rosters: a worker assists with morning personal care from 7am to 10am, is off duty and unpaid, then returns for evening support from 5pm to 8pm. That is a broken shift.

A broken shift can include up to three periods of work and two unpaid breaks, but the second break requires the employee's written agreement before the shift or as part of an agreed regular pattern. No agreement, no second break. Rostering one without it is a breach.

## Who the broken shift clause actually covers?

This is the detail most providers miss. Broken shifts under SCHADS apply only to home care employees providing services in clients' homes, and social and community services employees performing disability services work. Not all SACS employees. [Support coordinators](https://tesseractapps.com.au/solutions/support-coordination) and case managers doing non-disability work are not eligible.

The allowance also applies only to full-time and part-time employees. Casuals are excluded. Their 25% loading compensates for fragmented work patterns. Paying the allowance to a casual is an overpayment. Not paying it to an eligible permanent employee is an underpayment. Both directions create exposure.

## The 12-hour span rule: where most roster errors happen 

The total time between the start of the first work period and the end of the last must not exceed 12 hours. Any work performed beyond that span is paid at double time, regardless of how many hours the employee actually worked that day.

This is what catches providers out. A worker who starts at 8am, takes a four-hour unpaid break, and finishes at 9pm has a 13-hour span. The final hour attracts double time even if total hours worked is only eight. The trigger is the span, not the hours. Providers who roster around shift length without tracking the span will breach this regularly.

Employees working broken shifts on consecutive days must also receive a minimum 10-hour break between shifts. Eight hours if the preceding shift included a sleepover.

## How the broken shift allowance works?

The allowance compensates for the inconvenience of fragmented work and sits on top of, not instead of, the applicable hourly and penalty rates. A broken shift on a Saturday attracts both the Saturday penalty on the hours worked and the broken shift allowance. They are independent entitlements.

From 1 July 2025, the amounts are:

- $20.82 per shift for one unpaid break
- $27.56 per shift for two unpaid breaks (written employee agreement required)

These are per shift per day, not per break. Both amounts are indexed annually alongside base rates and will update from 1 July 2026. Each work period within the broken shift must also meet the two-hour minimum engagement rule. A worker cannot be brought in for 45 minutes, stood down, and called back. Each block is a minimum of two hours.

## A practical rostering example 

A support worker delivering NDIS community access works two blocks: 7am to 9am and 5pm to 8pm. The span from first start to last finish is 13 hours, which breaches the 12-hour limit. The final hour would attract double time.

The fix is straightforward: shift the morning block to 8am to 10am, bringing the span to exactly 12 hours. A 7am start with a 7pm finish also works if the evening block ends earlier. If that same worker is permanent and delivering disability support services, the $20.82 broken shift allowance applies on each day the pattern runs. If they are casual, it does not, regardless of how fragmented the day looks. And if the pattern runs on consecutive days, the gap between 8pm on day one and 8am on day two is exactly 12 hours, right on the minimum. A 9pm finish would drop that rest period to 11 hours, still compliant. A 10pm finish gets it to 10 hours, the floor.

## Common mistakes NDIS providers make 

Applying the allowance to all SCHADS staff. The broken shift rules do not cover everyone under the award. Paying it to ineligible roles is an overpayment that is awkward to unwind.

Confusing meal breaks with broken shift gaps. A standard unpaid lunch does not trigger the clause. The worker must be genuinely released from duty for an extended unpaid period between separate engagements.

Tracking hours instead of span. A worker doing six hours across a 13-hour span has still breached the award. Double time applies to the final hour regardless of actual hours worked.

Missing the allowance entirely. It does not appear automatically in most payroll systems unless it has been configured to trigger. Many providers simply do not know it exists until an audit surfaces it.

## How purpose-built rostering helps? 

Managing span limits, consent requirements and allowance triggers manually across a full week's roster is where errors quietly accumulate. Each shift looks fine in isolation. It is the combination, the span from 7am to 9pm, the same worker on consecutive days, the casual who should not be getting the allowance, that is hard to track without a system that understands the award rules.

[TesseractApps ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/)flags broken shift breaches directly in the rostering module as shifts are built, before the roster is published rather than discovered in payroll two weeks later. Because rostering, timesheets and payroll sit on one platform, the broken shift allowance flows straight through to the payslip without anyone calculating it separately or remembering to add it. The span check, the consent flag and the allowance trigger are built into the roster, not bolted on after. See the full compliance picture on the SCHADS guide or try the rostering module to see how it handles your specific shift patterns.

### Broken shifts under SCHADS FAQ 

Who is eligible for the broken shift allowance? 

Full-time and part-time home care employees, and SACS employees performing disability services work. Casual employees are excluded.

What is the broken shift allowance in 2026? 

$20.82 per shift for one unpaid break, $27.56 for two (with written employee agreement). Both update with the annual wage review from 1 July 2026.

What is the maximum span for a broken shift? 

12 hours from the start of the first work period to the end of the last. Hours beyond that are paid at double time.

Does a meal break count as a broken shift? 

No. A standard unpaid meal break during a continuous shift does not trigger the clause.

How much rest is required between broken shifts on consecutive days?

A minimum of 10 hours. Eight hours if the preceding shift included a sleepover.



This guide is general information only and does not constitute legal or workplace relations advice. Confirm your obligations with the Fair Work Ombudsman on 13 13 94.

# SCHADS Award 2026: The Complete Guide for NDIS and Disability Providers 

SCHADS Award rates rose 4.75% from 1 July 2026. Plain-English guide to pay rates, classifications, penalties and allowances for NDIS and disability providers. 

Most operations managers know the SCHADS Award exists. Fewer know it well enough to catch a classification error before it becomes a backpay liability. The Fair Work Commission confirmed a 4.75% increase to all SCHADS Award minimum pay rates on 2 June 2026, effective from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026, not from 1 July itself. That distinction catches providers out every year.

This guide covers the award in plain English: what it includes, how SCHADS classifications work, the updated pay rates, and what the 2026 changes mean for NDIS workforce compliance.

## What is the SCHADS Award? 

The SCHADS Award, formally the Social, Community, Home Care and Disability Services Industry Award 2010 (MA000100), sets legally enforceable minimum wages and conditions for more than 250,000 workers across disability, home care, aged care and community services in Australia. It is made by the Fair Work Commission and enforced by the Fair Work Ombudsman.

People still call it the social and community services award, which is actually one of four streams inside it.

For an NDIS provider, the award almost certainly covers your support workers, personal carers, community access staff, support coordinators, recovery coaches and case managers. It is also, without much competition, one of the most complex awards in the country. Eight classification levels, four streams, multiple pay points within each level, and penalty rate, [broken shift](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches), [sleepover ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel)and travel allowance provisions that interact differently depending on the type of work being performed. Getting one thing wrong means getting it wrong every fortnight.



## What changed for 2026 and why it matters more than usual ?

The headline is 4.75%. Every SCHADS minimum rate goes up by that figure from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026. Last year's increase was 3.5%, so this year's jump is steeper.

On the same day, the Superannuation Guarantee rate moves to 12%. Your actual on-cost per worker rises by more than the wage number alone suggests. If you are running thin margins between what NDIS price limits allow and what it costs to deliver a shift, July 2026 is a month to model carefully.

Two other changes landed around the same time. From 1 June 2026, following the Fair Work Commission's decision in [2025] FWCFB 292, work performed immediately before and after a sleepover is treated as a single continuous shift for overtime purposes. Payroll settings and written sleepover agreements needed updating before that date. If you also deliver aged care, watch 1 August 2026, when home care employees under Schedule E may move again under the aged care Work Value case. That second date is easy to miss.

## SCHADS classifications: where most underpayments actually start? 

Here is the thing about SCHADS classifications that does not get said enough: the level is set by what a worker does, not what their contract says or what qualification they hold. A worker with a degree performing Level 2 duties is paid at Level 2. A Certificate III holder performing Level 3 duties is entitled to Level 3 pay. The Fair Work Ombudsman's compliance activity consistently shows misclassification, usually downward, as one of the most common underpayment causes in the sector.

A worker's classification is determined by three inputs: qualifications (Certificate III, Certificate IV, diploma or degree), the duties they actually perform day to day, and their experience. Duties carry the most weight.

The award runs across four streams. The Social and Community Services (SACS) stream covers case management, support coordination, recovery coaching and community development. It is the most common stream for NDIS coordination roles, and the one most often misapplied to direct support workers. The Disability Services stream covers direct support work, personal care and community access. If your support workers are delivering NDIS funded services in participants' homes or the community, this is almost certainly their stream, not SACS. The Home Care stream covers home care workers and domestic assistants, and Crisis Accommodation covers refuge and crisis support roles.

Within each level sit pay points that workers progress through over time. A Level 3 at pay point 1 and a Level 3 at pay point 3 are meaningfully different wages. Misread the stream or the pay point and the error runs on every single pay cycle.

## SCHADS pay rates 2026 

The table below shows indicative full-time and part-time hourly rates for the SACS stream after the 4.75% increase. Use them for budgeting, and confirm exact figures against the Fair Work Ombudsman's MA000100 pay guide once updated for the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026.

Under the indicative 2026 SCHADS Award hourly rates, **Level 2 employees are paid around $36.20 per hour, Level 3 employees around $40.50 per hour, and Level 4 employees around $46.70 per hour at Pay Point 1.**

Casual employees receive a 25% loading on top of the base rate in place of paid leave entitlements. That loading does not stack on top of overtime rates. Do not apply SACS rates to Disability Services or Home Care workers. The streams have different tables, and conflating them is a common source of error.

## Penalties and allowances: the part that surprises most managers 

Base rates are the floor. What actually gets paid on any given shift depends on when it falls, how it is structured, and what the worker does during it.

[Penalty rates apply outside ordinary hours](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates), broadly Monday to Friday between 6am and 8pm, escalating on evenings, nights, Saturdays, Sundays and public holidays. [Overtime works differently by stream](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates): SACS and crisis accommodation employees are on 150% for the first three hours and 200% beyond that, while disability services and home care employees move to 200% after just two hours. Sunday overtime is double time. [Public holiday overtime](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-overtime-penalty-rates) is double time and a half.

Allowances catch a lot of providers out. [Broken shift allowances apply](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-broken-shifts-rostering-without-breaches) when a shift contains an unpaid break. [Sleepovers carry a specific allowance](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-sleepover-active-hours-travel) of 4.9% of the standard rate for each continuous eight-hour sleepover period, plus overtime rates for any active work overnight. Staff driving between clients in their own car are entitled to a per-kilometre vehicle allowance. There are also [minimum engagement rules](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-minimum-engagement): SACS employees must be paid for a [minimum of three hours per shift](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-minimum-engagement), most others for two. A worker who does 90 minutes is still owed the three-hour minimum on the SACS stream.

### Worked example: what a Saturday visit actually costs 

Take a permanent Level 2 SACS worker on an indicative base of around $36.20 an hour. Saturday work attracts a penalty lifting the rate to roughly $54.30 before allowances. Apply the three-hour minimum engagement and a 90-minute visit costs around $163 in wages alone, before super, travel or admin. That is the gap between the NDIS weekend price limit and your delivery cost, and it is why shifting non-urgent supports to weekdays is one of the more practical ways to protect a participant's budget and your margin at the same time.

## SCHADS and NDIS pricing: the link providers often underestimate 

The NDIA's Disability Support Worker Cost Model sits behind the [NDIS Pricing Arrangements](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/ndis-pricing-arrangements-2026-27) and is built on SCHADS rates. When SCHADS goes up, your cost of delivering supports rises from 1 July. The price limit you can claim only adjusts on the NDIS pricing cycle, which does not always align. In that gap, you absorb the difference. Add super moving to 12% on the same day and the margin compression is real. In a sector running on tight unit economics, the July changeover warrants proper financial modelling, not just a payroll system update.

The compliance exposure runs the other direction too. [Underpayments under the Fair Work Act](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-breaches-fair-work-software-prevention) can be backdated, the Ombudsman can investigate, and [NDIS quality audits](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-audit-guide-self-assess-fair-work) increasingly check that [rostering records, timesheets, payroll and claiming data](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately) all reconcile. [Auditors ask how SCHADS is interpreted](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/schads-award-audit-guide-self-assess-fair-work) and whether that interpretation is documented. "It's in our payroll system somewhere" does not satisfy an auditor.

## What to actually do before 1 July ?

Four things, in order. Audit every worker classification against current duties, not the duties listed when they were onboarded. Roles drift. Classifications often do not. Update your payroll system for the 4.75% wage increase and the 12% super rate, both from the first full pay period on or after 1 July 2026. Check that rostering surfaces penalty rates, broken shift allowances, minimum engagement and overtime before a shift is published, not in the payroll run two weeks later. And make sure your [rostering and payroll systems](https://tesseractapps.com.au/blog/how-ndis-providers-track-employee-hours-accurately) actually talk to each other, because re-keying hours between two systems is where rates go stale and errors propagate.

[TesseractApps ](https://tesseractapps.com.au/)interprets SCHADS award rules inside the rostering tool as shifts are built, then carries those hours directly through to payroll without double handling. One update to the pay rates cascades through rostering, timesheets, claiming and audit evidence. See how it fits together on our SCHADS compliance page.

### Before the first pay run 

July comes around the same time every year. The providers that handle it well treat the wage review as a real operational deadline: classifications checked, rates updated, systems reconciled, before the first pay period closes. The ones that do not tend to find out through a payroll dispute or an audit, both of which cost significantly more than the preparation would have.

This guide is general information only and does not constitute legal or workplace relations advice. Confirm current rates and your obligations with the [Fair Work Ombudsman](https://www.fairwork.gov.au/) on 13 13 94 and the official MA000100 pay guide.

Tesseractapps builds SCHADS award interpretation directly into rostering and payroll for NDIS providers. Visit [tesseractapps.com.au](https://tesseractapps.com.au) to see how it works.

# Platform Providers: Are You Affected by the New NDIS Registration Rules?

NDIS platform providers must register from 1 July 2026. Find out if your platform is affected and what registration requires.

If you run a digital platform that connects NDIS participants with support workers, you need to read this. The December 2025 announcement from NDIS Minister Jenny McAllister confirmed that platform providers, not just SIL providers, must register with the NDIS Commission from 1 July 2026.

This is a significant change that many platform operators are not yet aware of. Here is what it means, who is affected, and what you need to do.

## Who Counts as a Platform Provider?

The term 'platform provider' refers to organisations that connect NDIS participants with support workers or service providers through a digital marketplace or platform model. If your business operates a website, app, or online system where participants find and book support workers, and you take a fee or margin from that transaction, you are likely captured by this definition.

The Commission is expected to provide more detailed guidance on transition arrangements in early 2026, but the direction is clear: if your platform touches NDIS funding, registration is coming.

## Why Platform Providers Are Being Brought In

The push to include platform providers in mandatory registration comes from participant safety concerns. The platform model has grown rapidly in the NDIS, and with it came reports of inconsistent support quality, inadequate worker screening, and limited recourse for participants when things went wrong.

Mandatory registration brings platform providers under the same Practice Standards framework as other registered providers, including requirements for worker screening, incident reporting, governance, and quality management.

## What Registration Will Require for Platform Providers

While the specific registration requirements for platform providers are still being finalised, they are expected to align with the broader Practice Standards framework. At a minimum, plan to demonstrate:

- A governance structure with documented accountability
- Worker screening verification for all workers connecting through your platform
- An incident management system with reportable incident capability
- A complaints and feedback mechanism accessible to participants
- A risk management framework appropriate to your service model
- Policies and procedures aligned to the relevant Practice Standards

## The Worker Screening Challenge for Platforms

For many platform providers, worker screening is the most complex piece of the registration puzzle. Unlike traditional providers who employ workers directly, platforms often work with independent contractors. Verifying and maintaining current screening for a large, distributed workforce requires a systematic approach, not a manual one.

Platform providers who do not yet have a centralised system for tracking worker screening status, credential expiry, and compliance history will need to build one before registration.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Q: What is an NDIS platform provider?

A: An NDIS platform provider is an organisation that connects participants with support workers through a digital marketplace, website, or app and takes a fee or margin from the transaction.

### Q: Do NDIS platform providers need to register?

A: Yes. From 1 July 2026, all platform providers must register with the NDIS Commission under the mandatory registration requirements.

### Q: What is the biggest challenge for platform provider registration?

A: Worker screening is typically the most complex requirement, because platforms often work with independent contractors rather than direct employees, making credential verification at scale challenging.

## How to Prepare if You Are a Platform Provider

- Confirm your legal status: seek advice on whether your platform model falls within the Commission's definition of a platform provider.
- Map your current governance structure and identify gaps against the Practice Standards.
- Audit your worker screening processes: can you verify current screening status for every worker on your platform right now?
- Review your incident management capability: do you have a system to capture, investigate, and report incidents involving workers connected through your platform?
- Engage early with the Commission's transition guidance, expected in early 2026.

## The Opportunity in Registration

It is easy to see mandatory registration as a burden: more paperwork, more cost, more compliance overhead. But for platform providers who embrace it, registration is also a quality signal. Participants and their families increasingly check registration status before choosing a provider. Being registered tells them you have met an independently verified standard of quality and safety.

The platform providers who prepare early and genuinely build their operations around the standards will be better positioned in a market where quality is increasingly the differentiator.

# NDIS SIL Co-Design Standards: How Participants Are Shaping the New Rules

The new NDIS SIL Practice Standard is being co-designed with participants through Inclusion Australia. Learn what this means for providers.

Something different is happening with the new SIL Practice Standard, and it is worth paying close attention to. Rather than having regulators write standards in isolation and hand them down to the sector, the NDIS Commission has partnered with Inclusion Australia to co-design the new standard with participants at the centre.

This is not just a feel-good policy approach. It has real implications for what the standard will require, how providers will be assessed, and what participants will increasingly expect from their SIL providers.

## What Co-Design Actually Means in This Context

Co-design, in this context, means that people with disability have been active participants in shaping what the standard looks like, not just consulted after the fact. The Commission partnered with Inclusion Australia, a national organisation representing people with intellectual disability, to ensure that the voices of people who actually live in SIL settings informed the standard's direction.

The Commission's consultation process involved more than 800 stakeholders in 2024, generating an Insights Report that captured what participants and their families believe is most important in housing and living supports.

## What Participants Said They Want

The Insights Report from the 2024 consultation provides a clear picture of participant priorities. Across the submissions, a consistent set of themes emerged:

- Choice and control in day-to-day decisions, not just in the support planning process
- Staff who are consistent, trustworthy, and genuinely understand their support needs
- Clear and accessible information about their rights and how to raise concerns
- Providers who actively involve them in decisions about their living arrangements
- Supports that help them connect with their communities, not just meet their care needs

## What This Means for SIL Providers in Practice

If participant feedback is genuinely shaping the new standard, providers can expect the standard to focus heavily on:

- Individualised support planning: Generic support plans will not pass audit. Each plan must reflect the individual's actual goals, preferences, and needs.
- Feedback and grievance mechanisms: Providers will need to demonstrate not just that a complaints policy exists, but that participants know how to use it, feel safe doing so, and can see that their feedback leads to action.
- Workforce culture: The standard is expected to address how providers foster a workforce culture that respects participant autonomy and builds genuine relationships.
- Community participation: Supports that keep participants isolated in their homes will not align with what participants have said they want.

## Why This Is Good News for Quality Providers

If you are already running a participant-centred service, if your staff genuinely know and respect the people they support, if your plans are individualised, if your participants feel heard, then the new standard is essentially validating the way you already work. The challenge will be documenting it in a way that auditors can verify.

The providers who will struggle are those who have treated compliance as a paperwork exercise while the quality of actual support has lagged behind. The new standard is designed to make that gap visible.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Q: What does co-design mean in the NDIS context?

A: Co-design means people with disability actively participate in shaping policies and standards that affect them, rather than being consulted after decisions are made.

### Q: Who is Inclusion Australia?

A: Inclusion Australia is a national organisation representing people with intellectual disability. The NDIS Commission partnered with them to co-design the new SIL Practice Standard.

### Q: How will co-design affect NDIS providers?

A: Providers can expect stronger requirements around individualised support planning, participant feedback mechanisms, workforce culture, and community participation.

## How to Prepare for a Co-Designed Standard

- Talk to your participants now: ask them what is working and what is not, and document the conversations.
- Review your support plans with fresh eyes: are they genuinely individualised, or templates with names swapped?
- Audit your feedback mechanisms: do participants actually know how to raise a concern? Do they feel safe doing so?
- Look at your workforce culture honestly: would your participants describe their support workers as consistent, respectful, and genuinely caring?
- Ensure your documentation system can show evidence of participant involvement, not just staff activity.

# Mandatory SIL Registration from 1 July 2026: Your Complete Checklist

Mandatory NDIS SIL registration starts 1 July 2026. Download our complete registration readiness checklist and prepare step by step.

On 1 July 2026, the rules change. Supported Independent Living (SIL) providers who have operated outside the NDIS registration system will no longer be able to do so. The NDIS Minister confirmed this in December 2025, and it represents one of the most significant structural shifts the disability sector has seen.

If you are currently unregistered or unsure of your status, this is your definitive guide to what NDIS SIL mandatory registration involves, what you need to have in place, and how to avoid last-minute scrambling.

## Why Mandatory Registration Is Happening

The push for mandatory SIL registration comes directly from the 2023 NDIS Review and subsequent stakeholder consultations. Participants and families reported significant variation in the quality of SIL supports, and a lack of oversight for unregistered providers was identified as a key risk. Mandatory registration brings all SIL providers under the Commission's regulatory framework for the first time.

Platform providers, organisations that connect participants with support workers through digital platforms, are also required to register under the same deadline.

## What NDIS SIL Registration Requires

To become a registered NDIS provider, you must meet the requirements of the NDIS Practice Standards relevant to your registration group. For SIL providers, this includes a new dedicated SIL standard currently being finalised. At a high level, you will need to demonstrate:

- A governance structure with clear accountability
- Documented policies and procedures aligned to the Practice Standards
- A risk management framework with active monitoring
- Worker screening and credential verification processes
- An incident management system with reporting capability
- A business continuity plan
- Participant feedback mechanisms and continuous improvement processes

## Your Registration Readiness Checklist

Our Registration Readiness Checklist covers six key areas: governance, policies and procedures, workforce requirements, incident management, participant supports, and quality systems. Each section includes specific items to verify before you submit your application.

## Registration Timeline: What to Do and When

Now (June 2026)  —  Complete a gap analysis against the Practice Standards checklist

Weeks 1–4  —  Update policies, procedures, and governance documentation

Weeks 5–8  —  Complete staff training; verify worker screening status

Weeks 9–12  —  Run an internal audit to identify remaining gaps

Before 1 July  —  Submit registration application with all supporting evidence

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Q: When does mandatory NDIS SIL registration start?

A: 1 July 2026. All SIL providers must be registered by this date with no grace period.

### Q: How long does NDIS provider registration take?

A: Registration typically takes 8–12 weeks from application to certification. Starting early is essential.

### Q: What happens if I am not registered by July 2026?

A: Unregistered SIL providers will not be able to deliver NDIS-funded supports after 1 July 2026.

### Q: Are platform providers also required to register?

A: Yes. Platform providers that connect participants with support workers must also register by 1 July 2026.

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

- Assuming the process is quick. Registration typically takes 8–12 weeks from application to certification.
- Treating documentation as a one-time exercise. Auditors want to see evidence of ongoing monitoring, not just a document written the day before the audit.
- Underestimating workforce requirements. Every worker needs current screening and training records.
- Using paper-based or spreadsheet systems that cannot produce audit-ready evidence quickly.

## How Software Makes Registration Manageable

The volume of documentation required for NDIS registration is significant. Providers who try to manage this across paper files, shared drives, and spreadsheets consistently report the same problem: they know the information exists somewhere, but they cannot produce it quickly when an auditor asks.

Purpose-built NDIS compliance software keeps all of this in one place: policies, worker credentials, incident records, participant feedback, and audit logs, so that registration is a matter of exporting evidence, not hunting for it.

# NDIS Business Continuity Plan Requirements 2026: What Auditors Expect

The 2026 NDIS Practice Standards raise the bar for business continuity plans. Learn what auditors now expect and how to make your BCP audit-ready.

Business continuity planning has always been a requirement for registered NDIS providers. But the 2026 Practice Standards update has significantly raised the bar, and the gap between what providers have on paper and what auditors now expect is wider than many realise.

This post explains exactly what auditors are looking for in a business continuity plan, what the common gaps are, and how to make sure your plan is audit-ready.

## What Has Changed

The updated standards go further than previous versions, specifically requiring providers to demonstrate three things that were previously vague or assumed:

- A clear, documented business continuity plan
- A participant communication strategy: what you will tell participants and their families if service delivery is disrupted
- Staff training for critical incidents: not just a policy, but evidence that staff have completed the training and know how to respond

The shift is from having a document to demonstrating a system. Auditors are not just asking to see your BCP; they are asking how it works in practice.

## What a Compliant BCP Looks Like in 2026

### Section 1: Risk Scenarios

Your plan must identify specific risks to service continuity, not generic categories like "natural disaster". What specific events could disrupt your service? Staff illness, IT failure, loss of premises, utility interruption? Each scenario needs a likelihood and impact assessment.

### Section 2: Response Protocols

For each risk scenario, document the specific response: who does what, in what order, with what resources. Include escalation pathways and alternative service delivery arrangements.

### Section 3: Participant Communication

This is the section most providers are missing. The 2026 standards require a documented protocol for how and when you will communicate with participants and their families during a service disruption. Templates for emails, SMS, or phone scripts should be prepared in advance.

### Section 4: Recovery and Review

How will you restore normal service? How will you capture lessons learned? How will you update the plan based on what happened? These are the questions auditors will ask.

## Staff Training Requirements

Having a BCP is one thing; having staff who know what to do is another. The updated standards require evidence of critical incident training:

- All staff complete training that covers your specific BCP protocols
- Training completion is recorded and kept up to date
- New staff complete training as part of induction
- Refresher training occurs at least annually or when the plan is updated

The most common audit finding in this area is providers who have a training policy but cannot produce records showing that training actually occurred.

## Common Audit Failure Points

Generic scenarios  -  Plans list "natural disaster" without specifying what that means for your specific service.

Missing participant comms  -  No documented protocol for how and when to notify participants of service disruption.

No training records  -  BCP training policy exists but staff records do not show completion.

Untested plans  -  Plan has never been reviewed, tested, or updated since first written.

No ownership  -  No named person responsible for maintaining and implementing the plan.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Q: What must an NDIS business continuity plan include in 2026?

A: A compliant BCP must include specific risk scenarios, documented response protocols, a participant communication strategy, staff training records, and a recovery and review process.

### Q: Do NDIS auditors check BCP training records?

A: Yes. Auditors expect evidence that all staff have completed BCP-specific training, with completion dates recorded. A policy alone is not sufficient.

### Q: How often should an NDIS BCP be reviewed?

A: At least annually, and whenever the plan is updated or a significant incident occurs. Document every review.

## How to Make Your BCP Audit-Ready

- Assign a named BCP owner: a specific person, not a role title, responsible for maintaining the plan.
- Schedule a BCP review at least annually and document it.
- Run a tabletop exercise: walk your leadership team through a scenario and test whether the plan works.
- Build participant communication into your BCP from the start, not as an afterthought.
- Use a software system that stores your BCP, training records, and incident history in one place so you can produce audit evidence in minutes.

# NDIS Practice Standards Review 2026: What SIL Providers Need to Know

The NDIS Practice Standards review brings major changes for SIL providers from 1 July 2026. Understand what is changing, why it matters, and how to prepare.

If you provide Supported Independent Living (SIL) supports under the National Disability Insurance Scheme, the next 12 months will reshape how your service is regulated. The NDIS Quality and Safeguards Commission is conducting its most significant review of the Practice Standards in years, and the outcomes will directly affect every registered SIL provider in Australia.

This guide explains exactly what the NDIS Practice Standards review covers, what the confirmed changes mean for SIL providers operationally, and what steps you should take now to stay compliant ahead of the 1 July 2026 deadline.

## What Is the NDIS Practice Standards Review?

The NDIS Practice Standards set the benchmark for how all registered NDIS providers must deliver supports. They cover governance, risk management, participant rights, workforce management, and the quality of day-to-day support delivery.

In 2024, the Commission launched a major consultation process involving more than 800 stakeholders to gather feedback on the current standards, specifically around housing and living supports. The feedback was captured in a publicly available Insights Report, and the Commission is now using that feedback to guide updates.

The timing is significant: new SIL Practice Standards are planned to take effect from 1 July 2026, aligned with the mandatory registration deadline for SIL and platform providers.

## What Is Changing for SIL Providers?

### 1. A dedicated SIL Practice Standard is coming

Unlike the current framework, which applies general standards across all registration groups, the new reforms will introduce a dedicated SIL Practice Standard. This standard will address the specific risks and quality expectations for housing and living supports, including individualised support planning, participant choice and control, and community participation.

### 2. Mandatory registration is now confirmed

From 1 July 2026, all SIL providers must be registered with the NDIS Commission. There is no grace period. If you currently operate as an unregistered provider, you must complete the registration process before this date or risk being unable to deliver funded supports.

### 3. Business continuity planning is no longer optional

The updated standards require a documented business continuity plan (BCP) that includes participant communication strategies and staff training for critical incidents. Auditors will expect to see evidence that your BCP has been tested, not just written. Read our full guide on [what NDIS auditors now expect from your BCP](/blog/ndis-business-continuity-plan-audit-2026).

### 4. Governance and accountability expectations have increased

The sector has moved from assuming good governance to requiring providers to demonstrate it. Expect auditors to ask for board minutes, documented decision-making processes, and evidence of continuous improvement, not just policies on paper.

## Why This Matters for Your Operations

For many SIL providers, especially smaller organisations that have operated outside the registration system, this represents a significant operational shift. The documentation requirements alone can feel overwhelming if you have not built the underlying systems yet.

The Commission has been transparent about the direction of change. Consultation on policy development and market readiness activities commenced in early 2026, giving providers time to prepare, but only if they act now.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Q: When do the new NDIS Practice Standards take effect?

A: The new SIL Practice Standards are planned to take effect from 1 July 2026, aligned with the mandatory registration deadline for SIL and platform providers.

### Q: Do all SIL providers need to register?

A: Yes. From 1 July 2026, mandatory registration applies to all SIL providers. Unregistered providers will not be able to deliver NDIS-funded supports.

### Q: What is a SIL Practice Standard?

A: A dedicated set of quality and safety requirements specifically designed for Supported Independent Living providers, covering governance, participant supports, workforce management, and business continuity.

### Q: How can I prepare for the NDIS Practice Standards changes?

A: Start with a gap analysis against the updated requirements. Review your registration status, audit your governance documentation, map staff training records, and ensure your systems can produce audit-ready evidence on demand.

## What You Should Be Doing Right Now

- Review your current registration status and identify gaps against the new requirements.

Download the [Commission's Insights Report](https://www.ndiscommission.gov.au) and familiarise yourself with the direction of the new SIL standard.

- Audit your governance documentation: policies, procedures, incident management, and business continuity plans.
- Map your staff training records against the updated expectations for critical incident protocols.
- Assess whether your current software systems can produce the evidence auditors will look for.

## How NDIS Compliance Software Helps

One of the most common pain points for providers preparing for audits is documentation: pulling together evidence across multiple systems, spreadsheets, and paper files. A purpose-built NDIS compliance platform centralises your records so that when an auditor asks to see your incident management history or your business continuity plan, you can produce it in minutes, not days.

If your current system cannot do that, now is the time to evaluate alternatives.

The NDIS Practice Standards review is not something providers can afford to watch from the sidelines. With mandatory SIL registration confirmed for 1 July 2026 and a dedicated SIL standard in development, the compliance landscape is shifting fast. The providers who prepare now will be in a much stronger position when auditors come knocking.

# NDIS Invoicing Requirements Checklist: What Every Provider Needs to Know

Get NDIS invoicing wrong and your claims get rejected, your cash flow suffers, and your audit risk goes up.

If you have run a business outside the NDIS sector, you know how invoicing works. You deliver a service, you send an invoice, you get paid. The invoice needs a date, a description, an amount, and your ABN.

NDIS invoicing is different. Every claim is tied to a specific support item in the [NDIS Support Catalogue](/ndis-glossary). Every support item has a line item code, a unit of measure, a price limit, and a set of delivery conditions. Your invoice is not just billing for a service. It is a claim against a participant's approved plan funding, and it has to be structured correctly or it will be rejected.

For providers who are new to the scheme, or who are scaling quickly and relying on manual processes, the invoicing requirements can become a significant source of operational drag and cash flow delay. This article breaks down exactly what NDIS invoicing requires, what auditors look for, and what happens when you get it wrong.

## The NDIS Invoicing Checklist: What Every Invoice Must Include

Regardless of whether you are billing a self-managed participant, a [plan-managed participant](/solutions/support-coordination), or claiming directly through the NDIS portal for agency-managed participants, your invoice needs to contain the following:

### For all NDIS invoices:

1. Your organisation's name and ABN
2. The participant's full name and NDIS number
3. The date the support was delivered, not the invoice date
4. A description of the support matching the relevant NDIS support item
5. The NDIS support item code from the current [Support Catalogue](/ndis-glossary)
6. The unit of measure (hourly, daily, each)
7. The quantity of units delivered
8. The price per unit, which must not exceed the NDIS price limit for that item
9. The total amount claimed
10. Your payment details

### For plan-managed participants, additionally:

- The plan manager's name and contact details
- Reference to the relevant service agreement

Missing any of these elements can result in the invoice being rejected by the plan manager or the NDIA portal, which means delayed payment and additional administrative work to resubmit.

## The Most Common NDIS Invoicing Mistakes

### Using the wrong support item code

The NDIS Support Catalogue is updated regularly. Price limits change. Item codes are occasionally modified or retired. If you are working from an outdated catalogue, or if your team is selecting support items from memory, errors are inevitable. A claim lodged under the wrong support item will either be rejected or, worse, paid and then flagged in an audit.

### Claiming above the price limit

Every support item has a maximum price. Claiming above it, even by a small margin, results in rejection. If your prices are set manually and have not been updated since the last catalogue revision, you may be billing at rates that are no longer valid.

### Mismatched service dates

The date on your invoice should reflect when the support was delivered, not when the invoice was generated. A claim where the service date does not match the shift record raises an immediate red flag with plan managers and NDIA reviewers.

### Bulk invoicing without itemisation

Some providers send a single invoice covering multiple supports across a billing period without breaking down each support delivery individually. Many plan managers require itemised invoices, one line per support delivered.

### Not retaining the underlying shift records

The invoice is the claim. The shift record, the [timesheet](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment), the [case note](/capabilities/voice-notes), and the signed service delivery record are the evidence. If you cannot produce the underlying records when asked, the claim is unverifiable. In an audit, unverifiable claims are treated as unsubstantiated.

> A rejected invoice is not just a billing error. It is a cash flow problem. For smaller providers, delayed payment from a handful of rejected claims can create real financial pressure within a single pay cycle.

## What Auditors Actually Look for in Invoicing Records

When the NDIS Commission examines your invoicing records, they are not just checking that invoices exist. They are looking for consistency across three layers.

### Layer 1: The invoice itself

Does it contain all required fields? Are the support item codes correct? Does the price match the current catalogue? Is the participant's NDIS number accurate?

### Layer 2: The shift record

Does the [timesheet](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment) confirm that the support was delivered on the date claimed, for the duration claimed, by a worker rostered to that participant?

### Layer 3: The case note

Does the [case note](/capabilities/voice-notes) for that shift describe supports consistent with what was invoiced? If the invoice claims two hours of personal care but the case note describes a community outing, that is a discrepancy that will be investigated.

All three layers need to be consistent with each other. Providers who have strong invoicing but poor documentation, or strong case notes but no timesheet records, are still exposed.

> [!WARNING]
> Common audit triggers: Price limit exceedances even by small amounts. Support item codes that do not match the service agreement. Service dates absent from timesheet or attendance records. Gaps between invoice dates and service delivery of more than 90 days. Participant billing that continues after a service agreement has expired. Invoices for supports not listed in the participant's active plan.


## Self-Managed, Plan-Managed, and Agency-Managed: What Changes

**Self-managed participants** pay you directly from their own funds. The compliance burden still applies but the claim does not pass through a plan manager or the NDIA portal.

**Plan-managed participants** have a registered plan manager who processes claims on their behalf. You invoice the plan manager, not the participant. Plan managers often have their own formatting requirements or submission portals in addition to the NDIS requirements.

**Agency-managed participants** are funded directly through the NDIA. You claim through the NDIS myplace provider portal. The portal validates your claim against the participant's plan in real time. If the support item, price, or dates do not match what is in the plan, the claim is rejected at submission.

## Auto-Invoicing: What It Is and Why It Matters

Manual invoicing, generating [invoices from timesheets by hand](/capabilities/ndis-claiming-invoicing), entering support codes one by one, checking price limits against the current catalogue, is viable at small scale. At any meaningful volume, it is a bottleneck and a risk.

Auto-invoicing means your platform generates invoices automatically from confirmed, [approved shift records](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment). When a shift is delivered and approved, the invoice is created with the correct support item code pulled from the service agreement, the price applied from the current catalogue, the participant details populated from their profile, and the service date matched to the actual delivery.

This eliminates the category of error that comes from manual data entry. It also accelerates your billing cycle. Instead of processing invoices at the end of the month, they can be generated and submitted within days of service delivery, improving cash flow without any additional administrative effort.

## What Good Looks Like in Practice

The right invoicing workflow looks like this:

1. A service agreement is set up with the correct NDIS support item codes and price limits
2. A shift is delivered, clocked, and approved through your [timesheet workflow](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment)
3. The invoice is generated automatically from that approved shift, no re-entry
4. The invoice contains all required fields, pulled from participant and service agreement records
5. The invoice is submitted to the plan manager or NDIA portal
6. The invoice links back to the [underlying shift](/capabilities/rostering-scheduling) and [case note](/capabilities/voice-notes) for audit evidence
7. Payments reconcile automatically in [Xero](/capabilities/xero-integration) against outstanding invoices

TesseractApps is built on this workflow. Invoices are generated per support delivery, itemised, and linked to the shift record that backs them, creating the three-layer consistency auditors look for. Support Catalogue pricing is maintained within the platform. And every invoice connects to the timesheet and case note, with the whole system integrating directly with Xero for accounts receivable reconciliation.

- Auto-invoicing from approved shift records
- Current NDIS Support Catalogue pricing applied automatically
- Itemised per support delivery
- Linked to shift records and case notes for audit evidence
- Compatible with plan manager and NDIA portal submission
- Integrated with [Xero](/capabilities/xero-integration) for accounts receivable reconciliation

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does TesseractApps work with plan managers directly?

Yes. Invoices generated in TesseractApps can be submitted to plan managers in the format they require. The platform supports all three participant management types within the same system.

### What happens if a claim is rejected by the NDIA portal?

Rejection reasons are recorded and surfaced within the platform. The invoice can be corrected and resubmitted without having to rebuild it from scratch.

### How does auto-invoicing handle participants who cancel a shift?

A cancelled shift does not generate an invoice for delivered supports. If a cancellation fee applies under the service agreement, the platform generates the appropriate claim for the cancellation support item.

### How far back can I pull invoicing records for an audit?

All invoice and shift records are retained and searchable. During an audit, you can produce a complete billing history for any participant, worker, or date range.

### Does TesseractApps keep the NDIS Support Catalogue pricing current?

Yes. Pricing within the platform is maintained against the current Support Catalogue, reducing the risk of claims being rejected due to outdated rates.

### We use MYOB, not Xero. Is that supported?

TesseractApps integrates natively with Xero. If you are on MYOB or another accounting platform, speak to the team about your options during a demo.

title: "How NDIS Providers Can Track Employee Hours Accurately (and Stay Compliant)"

# How NDIS Providers Can Track Employee Hours Accurately (and Stay Compliant)

Inaccurate work hour tracking is one of the most common and most expensive problems in NDIS workforce management. Here's how to fix it properly.

Tracking employee work hours sounds straightforward. A worker starts a shift, finishes a shift, and someone records the hours. Simple.

Except in an NDIS context, it is not. The hours a worker is present matter less than the hours they are performing specific supports, with specific participants, under specific funding lines. A four-hour shift might contain thirty minutes of community access, two hours of personal care, and ninety minutes of household tasks, each potentially billed differently, each potentially requiring separate documentation.

Add [SCHADS Award](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment) complexity including [penalty rates](/ndis-glossary), allowances, broken shift provisions, and sleepover conditions, and tracking hours accurately becomes a compliance-critical function, not a simple HR task.

When it goes wrong, it goes wrong in two directions: workers are underpaid, or participants are overbilled. Neither is acceptable, and both carry consequences.

## The Most Common Ways NDIS Providers Get This Wrong

### Paper timesheets and manual entry

Paper is the highest-risk timesheet format in existence. It cannot be timestamped, it cannot be validated against the roster, it can be written retroactively, and it has to be manually transcribed into payroll. Every step in that chain is an opportunity for error.

### Workers self-reporting without verification

When workers submit their own hours without any cross-check against the rostered shift, no GPS verification, no supervisor confirmation, no system match, there is no mechanism to catch discrepancies. Small overstatements across a large workforce add up to significant payroll leakage.

### Rostered hours used as actual hours

Some providers pay based on rostered shifts rather than actual time worked. For shifts that run predictably, this might be fine. For a workforce where shift lengths vary, participants cancel, or workers finish early or late, it is a systematic inaccuracy.

### No differentiation by support type

If all hours in a shift are recorded as a single block, there is no way to correctly attribute costs to funding lines, bill the right NDIS support categories, or produce accurate reports for participants or plan managers. This directly affects invoicing accuracy.

> Paying from the roster instead of actual hours is not an efficiency. It is a liability. Either workers are underpaid, or participants are overbilled. Usually both.

## What Accurate Hour Tracking Actually Requires

Fixing the problem properly means building the right controls into the workflow, not adding more manual steps at the end.

### Clock-in and clock-out linked to the shift record

Workers should [clock in and out digitally](/capabilities/clock-in-out), with their recorded times automatically matched against the rostered shift. Discrepancies should surface for supervisor review, not silently pass through to payroll.

### GPS or location verification for community-based shifts

For workers delivering supports in participants homes or in the community, location-based verification provides a basic check that the worker was where they were supposed to be. This is about having an auditable record that the support was delivered.

### Support-type tagging within shifts

The platform should allow workers to log what they were doing during a shift, not just that they were present. This creates the data needed to accurately attribute hours to the right NDIS support categories.

### Supervisor approval before payroll

No hours should reach payroll without a supervisor review step. The supervisor should be able to see the rostered shift, the clocked hours, and any flagged discrepancies, and approve, reject, or amend before the data flows downstream.

### A locked record after approval

Once hours are approved and paid, the record should be immutable. Changes to historical records should require a formal amendment process with an audit trail, not a simple edit.

## The HR and Payroll Risk of Getting This Wrong

The Fair Work Act and the [SCHADS Award](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment) both carry significant obligations around accurate payment. Underpayment, even unintentional, can result in back-payment orders, penalties, and reputational damage. The Fair Work Ombudsman recovered over $532 million in underpaid wages in 2022-23, with the care and community services sector among the most investigated industries.

Beyond legal risk, inaccurate hours tracking creates internal friction. Workers who consistently receive incorrect pay do not stay. And from the NDIS billing side, hours that do not match delivered supports create audit risk. If your claimed hours do not reconcile with your timesheet records, you have a compliance exposure that no amount of good intention will fix in a Commission review.

## What Good Looks Like in Practice

The right hour-tracking workflow looks like this, regardless of the system you use:

1. Workers clock in digitally at shift start, with a location check for community-based supports
2. Clock-out is recorded digitally at shift end, matched automatically against the roster
3. Support types are tagged during or immediately after the shift
4. Any discrepancy between clocked and rostered hours is flagged to a supervisor
5. The supervisor reviews and approves or queries before the record is locked
6. Approved records flow directly to payroll with the correct [SCHADS rates](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment) applied
7. The same confirmed record generates the [participant invoice](/capabilities/ndis-claiming-invoicing)

In TesseractApps, workers clock in and out digitally on mobile, with GPS verification available for community-based shifts. Hours are matched against the rostered shift automatically. Discrepancies are flagged to supervisors before the pay run. Support types are recorded at the shift level for accurate NDIS billing. And approved timesheets flow directly into Xero with SCHADS rates applied, creating one record that drives payroll accuracy, participant billing accuracy, and compliance documentation simultaneously.

- Digital clock-in and clock-out matched to the roster
- GPS location verification for community-based supports
- Discrepancy flagging for supervisor review
- Support-type tagging for accurate NDIS billing
- Timesheet approval workflow before payroll
- Direct [integration with Xero](/capabilities/xero-integration)
- Immutable approved records with full audit trail

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What happens if a worker disputes their hours?

With a digital system, every clock-in and clock-out is timestamped and logged against the shift record. The supervisor approval is also recorded. That full trail is available immediately.

### Does the system work for workers without reliable internet in the community?

TesseractApps is mobile-accessible. For connectivity in specific environments, speak to the team about how the platform handles remote or low-signal scenarios during a demo.

### How does hour tracking connect to NDIS billing?

In TesseractApps, the confirmed shift record including support types and hours feeds directly into [invoice gen](/capabilities/ndis-claiming-invoicing)eration. The shift record is the billing record. There is no re-entry of data between timesheet approval and invoice creation.

### We have staff on both casual and part-time arrangements. Can the system handle both?

Yes. TesseractApps tracks employment type per worker and applies the relevant [SCHADS entitlements](/capabilities/timesheets-payroll-alignment) including minimum engagement, broken shift provisions, and casual loadings automatically.

### Can we run timesheet reports for a specific worker or participant?

Yes. Reporting by worker, participant, date range, or support type is available. This is also what you will need to produce during an NDIS audit or Fair Work review.

### Does TesseractApps integrate with payroll systems other than Xero?

TesseractApps integrates natively with Xero. Speak to the team about your specific accounting setup during a demo if you are on a different platform.
